title: AgenticFocus: Object-Preserving Mixed Reality Synthesis from Human FPV Video for Dexterous Humanoid Learning
summary: Human egocentric video is a scalable supervision source for humanoid policy learning, but current pipelines struggle with hand-object occlusion, oversimplified motion, or specialized capture hardware. We introduce AgenticFocus, a Mixed Reality synthesis pipeline that converts ordinary first-person-view human videos into robot-trainable demonstrations by restoring occluded object geometry, reconstructing full-hand motion, and retargeting it to a humanoid embodiment through camera-relative alignment and layered compositing. The resulting dataset pairs focused visual observations with synchronized robot actions and states. AgenticFocus achieves lower trajectory error and smoother wrist motion than cross-embodiment baselines, with SPARC scores of -5.18 versus -5.56 and -6.05.

AI.tldr: AgenticFocus is a Mixed Reality synthesis pipeline that converts ordinary first-person-view human videos into robot-trainable demonstrations by restoring occluded object geometry, reconstructing full-hand motion, and retargeting to a humanoid embodiment, achieving better trajectory accuracy and smoother motion than baselines.
AI.motivation: Human egocentric video is a scalable supervision source for humanoid policy learning, but current pipelines struggle with hand-object occlusion, oversimplified motion, or specialized capture hardware.
AI.method: AgenticFocus is a Mixed Reality synthesis pipeline that converts ordinary first-person-view human videos into robot-trainable demonstrations by restoring occluded object geometry, reconstructing full-hand motion, and retargeting it to a humanoid embodiment through camera-relative alignment and layered compositing.
AI.result: AgenticFocus achieves lower trajectory error and smoother wrist motion than cross-embodiment baselines, with SPARC scores of -5.18 versus -5.56 and -6.05.
AI.conclusion: AgenticFocus provides a scalable supervision source for humanoid policy learning from ordinary first-person-view videos.

title: FlowDAgger: Human-in-the-Loop Adaptation of Generative Robot Policies in Latent Space
summary: Pretrained generative robot policies based on flow matching and diffusion have achieved impressive results across a wide range of manipulation tasks. Yet real-world deployments routinely expose failure modes outside the pretraining distribution. Closing these gaps typically requires large-scale data collection or online reinforcement learning on physical hardware, which is impractical for rapid and safe adaptation. We present FlowDAgger, a sample- and compute-efficient method for adapting frozen generative robot policies from human interventions in latent space. Our key idea is action inversion: each human expert action is mapped to the noise that would have produced it under the frozen base policy, using reverse-time integration followed by local refinement. The resulting inverted noise provides supervision for a lightweight latent policy that steers the base model at deployment time, enabling rapid skill acquisition while preserving its behavioral priors. We evaluate FlowDAgger in simulation and on real-world bimanual and single-arm manipulation, adapting both action-head VLAs and world-action models from a handful of interventions. FlowDAgger outperforms supervised fine-tuning and latent-space RL baselines and preserves pretrained skills on held-out tasks, offering a practical path for adapting robot foundation models in the real world. Website: https://microsoft.github.io/FlowDAgger

AI.tldr: FlowDAgger enables sample-efficient adaptation of frozen generative robot policies from human interventions by inverting expert actions into noise latents that steer the base model, outperforming fine-tuning and latent-space RL baselines while preserving pretrained skills.
AI.motivation: Pretrained generative robot policies (flow matching/diffusion) fail outside their training distribution, but closing these gaps is impractical due to the need for large-scale data collection or online RL on physical hardware. A rapid, safe, and compute-efficient adaptation method is needed.
AI.method: FlowDAgger uses action inversion: mapping each human expert action to the noise that would have produced it under the frozen base policy via reverse-time integration and local refinement. This inverted noise supervises a lightweight latent policy that steers the base model at deployment while preserving behavioral priors.
AI.result: Outperforms supervised fine-tuning and latent-space RL baselines in simulation and real-world bimanual/single-arm manipulation tasks, while preserving pretrained skills on held-out tasks.
AI.conclusion: FlowDAgger offers a practical path for adapting robot foundation models in the real world, enabling rapid skill acquisition from a handful of human interventions without large-scale data collection or online RL on hardware.

title: SplatCtrl: Perception-Action Coupling via Gaussian Scene Representations and Reactive Robot Control
comment: Published in 2026 International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA). 8 pages, 8 figures
summary: Robotic manipulators excel in structured environments but face substantial challenges in unstructured and dynamic settings. This paper presents SplatCtrl, a unified framework for real-time scene reconstruction and reactive robot motion generation to enable collision-free robotic arm control in previously unseen and continuously changing environments. Building on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS), we introduce a hybrid voxel-based filtering and dynamic Gaussian relocation strategy that supports efficient scene reconstruction from RGB-D streams while accommodating environmental changes. For safe and reactive control, we further propose a method for deriving continuous signed distance functions from isotropic Gaussians, providing stable and differentiable collision probability estimates that bridge classical distance fields with the modern implicit representation. These continuous distance metrics are incorporated into control barrier functions, resulting in a unified perception-action coupling framework that supports smooth and reliable real-time motion generation in response to scene changes. Experimental validation in simulation, on physical robot, and within shared human-robot workspace demonstrates the framework's effectiveness, achieving integrated scene reconstruction and reactive control in uncertain, and dynamic environments.

AI.tldr: SplatCtrl is a unified framework that integrates 3D Gaussian Splatting-based real-time scene reconstruction with control barrier functions for reactive, collision-free robotic arm motion in dynamic and unstructured environments.
AI.motivation: Robotic manipulators struggle in unstructured and dynamic settings; existing methods lack seamless integration of real-time scene reconstruction and reactive motion generation for collision-free control.
AI.method: The framework combines (1) hybrid voxel-based filtering and dynamic Gaussian relocation for efficient RGB-D reconstruction via 3D-GS, (2) continuous signed distance functions derived from isotropic Gaussians for differentiable collision probability estimation, and (3) control barrier functions incorporating these distance metrics for unified perception-action coupling.
AI.result: Experimental validation in simulation, on physical robots, and in shared human-robot workspaces demonstrates effective integrated scene reconstruction and reactive control in uncertain, dynamic environments.
AI.conclusion: SplatCtrl enables smooth, reliable real-time motion generation responsive to scene changes, bridging classical distance fields with modern implicit neural representations for safe robotic control.

title: CLAP: Direct VLM-to-VLA Adaptation via Language-Action Grounding
summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) inherit semantic capabilities from pretrained VLMs, yet large-scale post-training on robot data and architectural modifications can reshape the backbone so extensively that it becomes difficult to isolate what the VLM contributes to control. Directly converting pretrained VLMs into VLAs with minimal architectural change offers a more transparent path to understanding how VLM capabilities transfer across model scales. The core obstacle is output-distribution mismatch: predicting actions as bare numeric token sequences moves generation away from the VLM's pretrained language distribution, degrading the capabilities we seek to preserve. To address this, we propose CLAP (Causal Language-Action Prediction), which prepends each numeric action sequence with a natural-language action description, causally conditioning precise action-token prediction on a language-action plan without modifying the backbone architecture. With single-epoch fine-tuning alone, 2B CLAP achieves 90.8% on LIBERO (+14.9 pt over VLA-0) and improves robustness on LIBERO-PRO under language, object, and spatial perturbations. We will release CLAP at 0.8B, 2B, and 4B as an open-weight, multi-scale compact VLA family from a single VLM lineage, enabling controlled analysis of VLM-to-VLA capability transfer.

AI.tldr: CLAP (Causal Language-Action Prediction) converts pretrained VLMs into VLAs by prepending natural-language action descriptions before numeric action tokens, preserving language-distribution capabilities and achieving 90.8% on LIBERO with minimal architectural changes.
AI.motivation: Existing VLAs undergo extensive architectural modifications and post-training that obscure how VLM capabilities transfer to control; a transparent method is needed to isolate VLM contributions across model scales without distribution mismatch.
AI.method: CLAP prepends each numeric action sequence with a natural-language action description, causally conditioning precise action-token prediction on a language-action plan without modifying the backbone VLM architecture; uses single-epoch fine-tuning.
AI.result: 2B CLAP achieves 90.8% on LIBERO (+14.9 pt over VLA-0) and improved robustness on LIBERO-PRO under language, object, and spatial perturbations. Models at 0.8B, 2B, and 4B will be released.
AI.conclusion: CLAP provides a transparent, multi-scale VLA family from a single VLM lineage, enabling controlled analysis of VLM-to-VLA capability transfer while achieving strong performance with minimal architectural changes.

title: Interval Certifications for Multilayered Perceptrons via Lattice Traversal
summary: In this work we present a rigorous theoretical framework to a foundational problem of AI safety, namely adversarial robustness. In particular, we show that the adversarial robustness problem can be reduced to a lattice traversal problem. Each element of this lattice corresponds to an interval, i.e., an axis-aligned hyper-rectangle, containing an input point $\mathbf{x}$. Consider a multilayered perceptron classifier (MLP). An interval $I$ constitutes a sound certification if $\mathbf{x} \in I$ and $\mathbf{x}$ can be freely perturbed in $I$ without changing the MLP's prediction. Complementarily, an interval $I$ constitutes a complete certification if $\mathbf{x} \in I$ and when $\mathbf{x}$ moves outside of $I$ the MLP's prediction is guaranteed to change. While the sound certification problem corresponds to the well-studied adversarial robustness, complete certifications have not been examined in the literature. We develop lattice traversal operators, which we apply in a refine & verify iterative scheme. Using formal MLP verifiers, sound maximality and complete minimality are guaranteed. Moreover, we examine objective optimization problems. There we discover some interesting asymmetries. For complete certifications, the minimum solution is obtained in polynomial oracle calls. This does not hold for sound certifications, where we prove strong intractability results. Additionally, we examine optimization problems in symmetric intervals (i.e., $\ell_\infty$-spheres), where we provide logarithmic algorithms. Finally, we present an empirical evaluation, using the novel ParallelepipedoNN system.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes adversarial robustness in AI safety as a lattice traversal problem, introduces the novel concept of complete certification (complementary to standard sound certification), develops lattice traversal operators within a refine & verify scheme, proves strong intractability for sound certification optimization while achieving polynomial oracle complexity for complete certification, provides logarithmic algorithms for symmetric intervals, and presents empirical results via the ParallelepipedoNN system.
AI.motivation: To provide a rigorous theoretical framework for adversarial robustness—a foundational AI safety problem—by reducing it to a lattice traversal problem, and to introduce and analyze the previously unexamined concept of complete certification alongside the well-studied sound certification.
AI.method: The paper reduces adversarial robustness to a lattice traversal problem where each lattice element is an axis-aligned hyper-rectangle (interval). It defines sound certification (prediction unchanged within interval) and complete certification (prediction changes when moving outside interval). Lattice traversal operators are developed and applied in a refine & verify iterative scheme using formal MLP verifiers. Optimization problems are analyzed via complexity theory, with algorithms for symmetric intervals.
AI.result: Sound maximality and complete minimality are guaranteed via formal verifiers. For complete certification optimization, the minimum solution is obtained in polynomial oracle calls, while sound certification optimization is proven strongly intractable. Logarithmic algorithms are provided for optimization in symmetric (\(\ell_\infty\)) intervals. Empirical evaluation is conducted using the ParallelepipedoNN system.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a foundational theoretical framework connecting adversarial robustness to lattice traversal, revealing fundamental asymmetries between sound and complete certification optimization—the former is intractable while the latter is polynomially solvable—and provides practical algorithms validated empirically.

title: Dec-MARVEL: Decentralized Multi-Agent Exploration without Communication under Budget Constraints
summary: Multi-UAV exploration is often constrained by unreliable communication, limited field-of-view sensing (e.g., lightweight onboard camera), and finite travel budgets that require each robot to reserve enough budget to return to its base. We present Dec-MARVEL, a decentralized budget-aware exploration framework for communication-free teams with directional sensing. Rather than exchanging maps, goals, or messages, each robot coordinates through its incidental observations: any teammate trajectory within its field of view serves as a coordination signal. A graph-attention actor fuses local frontier geometry, teammate motion, and budget features to select return-feasible waypoint-heading actions. The actor is trained with phase-conditioned critics, a training-only task-oriented privileged critic, and a mixture-based budget curriculum. Across 900 held-out trials spanning three team sizes (2, 4, 8 robots) and three travel budgets (720, 800, 1024 meters) against four baselines, Dec-MARVEL achieves the highest or tied-highest exploration rate and lowest sensing overlap across all nine team-size budget configurations. Under our tightest 720m budget, it reaches 53%, 94%, and 100% success for 2, 4, and 8 robots, versus 37%, 83%, and 99% for the strongest baseline. Physical-robot experiments demonstrate successful sim-to-real transfer and real-world deployment of Dec-MARVEL.

AI.tldr: Dec-MARVEL is a decentralized, communication-free multi-UAV exploration framework using directional sensing. Robots coordinate via incidental observations (teammate trajectories within FOV) without exchanging messages. A graph-attention actor selects return-feasible waypoint-heading actions, trained with phase-conditioned critics and budget curriculum. It achieves superior exploration rates and lowest sensing overlap across diverse team sizes and budgets, with successful real-world deployment.
AI.motivation: Multi-UAV exploration is constrained by unreliable communication, limited FOV sensing (lightweight onboard cameras), and finite travel budgets requiring each robot to reserve enough budget to return to base. Existing methods rely on communication or shared maps, which are impractical under these constraints.
AI.method: Dec-MARVEL: (1) Decentralized coordination via incidental observations (teammate trajectories visible within FOV) rather than explicit communication. (2) Graph-attention actor network fuses local frontier geometry, teammate motion, and budget features to select return-feasible waypoint-heading actions. (3) Phase-conditioned critics and a training-only task-oriented privileged critic. (4) Mixture-based budget curriculum for training.
AI.result: Across 900 held-out trials (2/4/8 robots, 720/800/1024m budgets) vs. 4 baselines: highest/tied-highest exploration rate and lowest sensing overlap in all 9 configurations. At 720m budget: 53%/94%/100% success for 2/4/8 robots vs. 37%/83%/99% for best baseline. Sim-to-real transfer and real-world deployment validated.
AI.conclusion: Dec-MARVEL effectively addresses communication-free, budget-constrained multi-UAV exploration with directional sensing through decentralized coordination via incidental observations, achieving state-of-the-art performance and successful real-world deployment.

title: CogniConsole: Externalizing Inference-Time Control as a Formal Abstraction for Reliable LLM Interactions
comment: Revised version focusing on the CogniConsole system architecture and empirical evaluation of inference-time control probes (N=489)
summary: Reliability in large language model (LLM) systems is typically framed as a function of model capability. We challenge this by demonstrating that reliability is significantly influenced by \emph{inference-time control} -- the computational layer governing task framing and context selection. We introduce \emph{CogniConsole}, an architectural instantiation that externalizes this control into a structured interface combining programmatic coordination with bounded prompt-based reasoning. Through \emph{controllability-oriented probes} ($N=489$) in a multi-step interactive environment, we show that increasing structural scaffolding -- from unstructured to fully scaffolded -- \textbf{systematically reduces output variance and failure rates under a fixed model architecture}. Our results indicate that many observed failure modes, such as context drift and inconsistent constraint adherence, arise from under-specified control rather than insufficient capability. This work provides an empirical basis for treating inference-time control as a first-class abstraction, opening new directions for designing and evaluating LLM systems beyond scaling alone.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CogniConsole, an inference-time control architecture that reduces LLM output variance and failure rates through structured scaffolding, demonstrating that many failure modes stem from under-specified control rather than insufficient model capability.
AI.motivation: To challenge the prevailing assumption that LLM reliability is primarily a function of model capability, and to demonstrate that inference-time control (task framing and context selection) significantly influences reliability.
AI.method: CogniConsole externalizes control via a structured interface combining programmatic coordination with bounded prompt-based reasoning. Evaluated using controllability-oriented probes (N=489) in a multi-step interactive environment, comparing unstructured to fully scaffolded configurations under a fixed model architecture.
AI.result: Increasing structural scaffolding systematically reduces output variance and failure rates. Many failure modes (context drift, inconsistent constraint adherence) arise from under-specified control, not insufficient capability.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time control should be treated as a first-class abstraction for LLM system design and evaluation, opening new directions beyond scaling alone.

title: Vascular Geometry Characterization for AI-Based Endovascular Navigation
summary: Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) is a time-critical intervention for acute ischemic stroke; however, access remains limited due to a shortage of neuroradiologists and specialized centers. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers potential to automate endovascular navigation and improve accessibility, yet current models lack standardized frameworks to assess navigation difficulty for model training and evaluation. This study aims to identify vascular metrics associated with navigation difficulty and to develop an automated pipeline for quantitative vascular feature extraction, enabling future complexity grading. Vascular trees were segmented from computed tomography angiograms from 61 patients, and vascular metrics including aortic arch type, presence of bovine arch, vessel length, tortuosity, take-off angle, number of reverse curves, were measured using a custom pipeline. A Soft Actor-Critic RL algorithm was used for 120 s autonomous navigation. Outcomes were analyzed using both mixed effects linear and logistic regression. On the left side, the presence of a bovine arch and aortic arch type II/III increased navigation time by 30.19 s and 37.92 s, respectively, while greater tortuosity (\b{eta} = 118.20) further prolonged the procedure and reduced success probability. On the right side, type II/III arches extended procedure time by 45.94 s, while each additional reverse curve was associated with 3.96 s longer navigation time and lower probability of success. These findings demonstrate for the first time that MT agent navigation difficulty is strongly influenced by vascular geometry. The proposed automated pipeline enables objective and quantitative characterization of vascular features, providing a foundation for future development of standardized complexity grading and RL model evaluation, without aiming to demonstrate clinically generalizable autonomous navigation.

AI.tldr: This study identifies key vascular metrics (aortic arch type, bovine arch, tortuosity, take-off angle, reverse curves) associated with mechanical thrombectomy navigation difficulty using a Soft Actor-Critic RL agent, and develops an automated pipeline for quantitative vascular feature extraction to enable future complexity grading and RL model evaluation.
AI.motivation: Mechanical thrombectomy is time-critical but access-limited due to shortage of specialists; RL-based autonomous navigation could improve accessibility, but currently lacks standardized frameworks to assess navigation difficulty for model training and evaluation.
AI.method: Vascular trees were segmented from CT angiograms of 61 patients; vascular metrics (aortic arch type, bovine arch, vessel length, tortuosity, take-off angle, number of reverse curves) were extracted via a custom automated pipeline. A Soft Actor-Critic RL algorithm performed 120s autonomous navigation. Outcomes were analyzed using mixed effects linear and logistic regression.
AI.result: On the left side, bovine arch and type II/III aortic arch increased navigation time by 30.19s and 37.92s, respectively; greater tortuosity (β=118.20) prolonged procedure and reduced success. On the right side, type II/III arches extended time by 45.94s; each additional reverse curve added 3.96s and lowered success probability.
AI.conclusion: MT agent navigation difficulty is strongly influenced by vascular geometry. The automated pipeline enables objective, quantitative characterization of vascular features, laying groundwork for standardized complexity grading and RL model evaluation, though not yet demonstrating clinically generalizable autonomous navigation.

title: GATS: Graph-Augmented Tree Search with Layered World Models for Efficient Agent Planning
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have shown promise in multi-step planning tasks, but existing approaches like LATS (Language Agent Tree Search) and ReAct rely heavily on LLM inference during planning, leading to high computational costs and stochastic behavior. We present \textbf{GATS} (Graph-Augmented Tree Search), a planning framework that combines systematic UCB1-based tree search with a layered world model to eliminate LLM calls during inference while achieving superior planning performance. Our three-layer world model integrates: (L1) exact symbolic action matching, (L2) statistics learned from execution logs, and (L3) LLM-based prediction for unknown actions. On synthetic planning tasks with branching paths and dead-ends, GATS achieves \textbf{100\% success rate} compared to 92 % for LATS and 64\% for ReAct. On a comprehensive stress test spanning 12 challenging scenarios -- including coding workflows, web navigation, and long-horizon tasks -- GATS maintains \textbf{100\% success} while LATS drops to 88.9 % and ReAct to 23.9%. GATS requires \textbf{zero LLM calls per task} during planning (vs. 37 per task for LATS) and produces deterministic plans with zero variance across runs. Our results demonstrate that systematic search with learned world models can substantially outperform LLM-guided exploration for agent planning.

AI.tldr: GATS (Graph-Augmented Tree Search) eliminates LLM calls during planning by combining UCB1-based tree search with a three-layer world model (symbolic matching, learned statistics, LLM prediction), achieving 100% success rate across benchmarks while LATS drops to 88.9% and ReAct to 23.9%.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent planning approaches (LATS, ReAct) rely heavily on LLM inference during planning, causing high computational costs and stochastic behavior. The authors aim to eliminate LLM calls during inference while improving planning performance.
AI.method: GATS combines systematic UCB1-based tree search with a three-layer world model: L1 (exact symbolic action matching), L2 (statistics learned from execution logs), and L3 (LLM-based prediction for unknown actions).
AI.result: GATS achieves 100% success rate on synthetic planning tasks (vs. 92% LATS, 64% ReAct) and 100% on 12 challenging scenarios (vs. 88.9% LATS, 23.9% ReAct), requiring zero LLM calls per task during planning (vs. 37 for LATS) with zero variance.
AI.conclusion: Systematic search with learned world models can substantially outperform LLM-guided exploration for agent planning, eliminating inference costs while improving deterministic performance.

title: Residual Physics-Informed Neural Networks for High-Fidelity BLDC Motor Modeling
summary: Accurate dynamics modeling of Brushless DC (BLDC) motors is fundamental to high-performance robotic joint control. This paper presents a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) with a deep residual (ResNet) backbone that learns a continuous-time surrogate of the full six-state BLDC motor dynamics. Given simulation time, applied three-phase voltages, and excitation parameters as inputs, the network directly predicts all motor state variables -- rotor angle, angular velocity, three-phase currents, and winding temperature -- while simultaneously satisfying the governing electromechanical and thermal ODEs through a composite physics-data loss. A curriculum scheduling strategy gradually activates the physics penalty to prevent premature convergence. Training runs are completed in under two minutes on a standard CPU. Crucially, once trained, PINN inference achieves latencies of 0.1--22, mu s per query, up to 118x faster than conventional ODE solvers, making it suitable for real-time observer and control applications.

AI.tldr: A Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) with deep residual backbone learns continuous-time BLDC motor dynamics, achieving 118x faster inference than conventional ODE solvers while satisfying electromechanical and thermal ODE constraints.
AI.motivation: Accurate dynamics modeling of BLDC motors is fundamental to high-performance robotic joint control, but conventional ODE solvers are too slow for real-time observer and control applications.
AI.method: A PINN with deep residual (ResNet) backbone predicts all six BLDC motor states (rotor angle, angular velocity, three-phase currents, winding temperature) from simulation time, three-phase voltages, and excitation parameters, using a composite physics-data loss with curriculum scheduling for the physics penalty.
AI.result: Training completes in under 2 minutes on CPU; inference achieves 0.1-22 µs per query, up to 118x faster than conventional ODE solvers.
AI.conclusion: The PINN approach enables real-time observer and control applications by providing fast and accurate BLDC motor dynamics predictions.

title: Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench: Testing the Limits of Agents on Long-Horizon Terminal Tasks with Dense Reward-Based Grading
summary: AI agents have become capable of autonomously completing short, well-specified tasks. However, existing terminal benchmarks largely focus on simple problems that finish within minutes and are evaluated only by their final outcome. This setup overlooks intermediate progress and partial solutions, yielding sparse reward signals and an incomplete picture of agent capability. We introduce Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench, a terminal benchmark of 46 long-horizon tasks spanning nine categories, including experiment reproduction, software engineering, multimodal analysis, interactive games, and scientific computing. Each task follows a Terminal-Bench-style setup with a reference solution or simulation engine, but is further decomposed into fine-grained graded subtasks. This design enables dense intermediate rewards and partial credit, allowing evaluation to capture not only whether an agent reaches the final goal, but also how far it progresses on open-ended workflows. Tasks in Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench typically require hundreds of episodes and minutes to hours of execution, stressing long-horizon planning, long-context management, and iterative debugging rather than one-shot problem solving. We evaluate 15 frontier models and find that agents consume on average 9.9M tokens per task, with roughly 231 episodes and 85.3 minutes of execution time per run, making Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench more demanding than prior terminal-based benchmarks. Even the strongest tested model achieves 15.2% pass@1 at a partial-reward threshold of 0.95 and 10.9% at a perfect-reward threshold of 1.0, while the mean pass rate across models is 4.3% and 1.7% under the two thresholds, respectively. These results reveal headroom for improvement. We further analyze failure modes and error patterns, and release Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench to support future progress on long-horizon terminal agents.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench, a benchmark of 46 long-horizon terminal tasks with graded subtasks for dense reward signals, finding that even the best model achieves only 15.2% pass@1 at a 0.95 partial-reward threshold, revealing significant room for improvement in long-horizon agent capabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing terminal benchmarks focus on short, well-specified tasks evaluated only by final outcomes, which overlooks intermediate progress and partial solutions, yielding sparse reward signals and an incomplete picture of agent capability. This motivates the need for a benchmark that captures how far agents progress on open-ended, long-horizon workflows.
AI.method: Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench consists of 46 long-horizon tasks across nine categories (experiment reproduction, software engineering, multimodal analysis, interactive games, scientific computing), each following a Terminal-Bench-style setup with a reference solution or simulation engine, but decomposed into fine-grained graded subtasks to enable dense intermediate rewards and partial credit evaluation.
AI.result: Evaluated 15 frontier models; agents consume on average 9.9M tokens, ~231 episodes, and 85.3 minutes per run. The strongest model achieves 15.2% pass@1 at 0.95 partial-reward threshold and 10.9% at perfect-reward threshold of 1.0, with mean pass rates across models of 4.3% and 1.7% respectively.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark reveals significant headroom for improvement in long-horizon planning, long-context management, and iterative debugging for terminal agents. The authors release the benchmark to support future progress.

title: BeyondSight: Object Permanence for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
summary: Autonomous driving operates in partially observable environments where actors may become fully occluded by other vehicles or infrastructure. Most end-to-end driving systems implicitly couple actor existence to instantaneous observations, causing actor hypotheses to degrade or disappear during prolonged occlusion and removing potentially critical agents from downstream prediction and planning. We introduce BeyondSight, a permanence-aware end-to-end driving framework that decouples actor existence from observability by maintaining persistent actor hypotheses over time. BeyondSight propagates actor queries temporally and updates them with observation-conditioned evidence, enabling joint perception, prediction, and planning to reason about actors even when they are temporarily unobservable. To enable principled training and evaluation of persistence-aware models, we further introduce nuScenes-Permanence, an extension of nuScenes that provides supervision and observability-conditioned evaluation for unobservable actors. Experiments show that BeyondSight substantially improves reasoning under occlusion, increasing detection performance for unobservable actors from 0 to 0.249 mAP while reducing planning error from 0.61 to 0.54 L2avg. These results highlight object permanence as an important modeling principle for robust end-to-end autonomous driving.

AI.tldr: BeyondSight is a permanence-aware end-to-end driving framework that decouples actor existence from observability by maintaining persistent actor hypotheses over time, improving detection of unobservable actors (0→0.249 mAP) and reducing planning error (0.61→0.54 L2avg) on the newly introduced nuScenes-Permanence dataset.
AI.motivation: Autonomous driving systems operate in partially observable environments where actors become fully occluded. Existing end-to-end driving systems implicitly couple actor existence to instantaneous observations, causing actor hypotheses to degrade or disappear during prolonged occlusion, which removes potentially critical agents from downstream prediction and planning.
AI.method: BeyondSight maintains persistent actor hypotheses over time by propagating actor queries temporally and updating them with observation-conditioned evidence, enabling joint perception, prediction, and planning to reason about actors even when temporarily unobservable. The authors also introduce nuScenes-Permanence, an extension of nuScenes with supervision and observability-conditioned evaluation for unobservable actors.
AI.result: Detection performance for unobservable actors improved from 0 to 0.249 mAP; planning error reduced from 0.61 to 0.54 L2avg.
AI.conclusion: Object permanence is an important modeling principle for robust end-to-end autonomous driving, as it substantially improves reasoning under occlusion.

title: A Formalization of the Mean-Field Derivation of the Vlasov Equation: AI-Assisted Lean Formalization as a Strategy Game
comment: 26 pages, 4 figures. Lean 4 development, blueprint site, and agent logs: https://github.com/Hydrodynamical/Vlasov_Meanfield_Formalization
summary: We formalize a research result in the Lean 4 proof assistant by having a mathematician direct an AI system, and frame the activity as a formalization game. The objective is to turn a LaTeX document into Lean. The game is won when the development compiles, contains no sorry, and a machine check shows the target theorems rest on Lean's foundational axioms alone. Reuse is a second check, by a definition we introduce: whether the development yields a self-contained layer of general mathematics the wider library could absorb. The case study is a complete, axiom-clean formalization of well-posedness for the nonlinear Vlasov equation via Dobrushin's mean-field route -- existence, uniqueness, the stability estimate and mean-field limit, and a short-window superposition principle (weak solutions are Lagrangian). The human's role was to direct, not to write proofs: to scope the definitions, steer the decompositions, and triage the library's gaps; the AI agent executed. The formalization certifies the proof of each statement as written; whether the written statement is the intended theorem stays the mathematician's judgment. The optimal-transport machinery that fell out of the build (in particular, properties of the Wasserstein-1 metric and the Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality theorem) separates into a self-contained layer that compiles against Mathlib alone: about a sixth of the development (49 of 299 declarations), behind a 22-declaration interface with no reverse dependency. The headline theorems ran in about a week, the full development in about a month. We report the quantitative claims as observations of one game, not as general laws. The game's rules name no particular system, so the methodological framing is meant to outlast the tools of any one run.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes the well-posedness of the nonlinear Vlasov equation in Lean 4 using an AI agent directed by a human mathematician, framed as a "formalization game." The development compiles axiomatically clean, with reusable optimal-transport machinery separated into a self-contained layer (49/299 declarations behind a 22-declaration interface). The human scoped definitions and steered decompositions; the AI wrote proofs. Full development took ~1 month; headline theorems ~1 week.
AI.motivation: To establish a methodological framework (the formalization game) for turning LaTeX mathematical proofs into fully verified Lean 4 code, while assessing the interplay between human direction and AI execution in formalization, and demonstrating the feasibility of axiom-clean, reusable formalization of nontrivial PDE analysis (Vlasov equation) with optimal-transport tools.
AI.method: A human mathematician directs an AI agent to formalize a LaTeX document into Lean 4, with the game won upon compilation with no "sorry" and foundational axiom verification. Reuse is measured via a self-contained layer definition. The case study covers existence, uniqueness, stability, mean-field limit, and a superposition principle for the Vlasov equation via Dobrushin's route.
AI.result: Complete, axiom-clean formalization achieved in ~1 month (headline theorems in ~1 week). Optimal-transport machinery (Wasserstein-1 metric, Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality) separates into a self-contained layer (49/299 declarations) with a 22-declaration interface and no reverse dependency on the rest of the development.
AI.conclusion: The formalization game framework is a viable methodology for AI-assisted proof formalization. The human's role remains essential for judgment, scoping, and decomposition; AI executes. The reusable layer demonstrates that formalized mathematics can be structured for library absorption. The rules are system-agnostic and intended to outlast any particular tool.

title: TactiDex: A Real-World Tactile-Guided Benchmark for Human-Like Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Tactile feedback is fundamental to Hand-Object Interaction (HOI), governing contact formation, force regulation, and stable manipulation, making it essential for achieving true human-like dexterous manipulation. Yet, current human-to-robot dexterous transfer pipelines primarily rely on kinematic trajectories, resulting in motion imitation without physically grounded interaction. To address this, we introduce TactiDex, a real-world tactile-guided benchmark specifically designed to move dexterous manipulation beyond kinematic mimicry toward contact-level human-likeness. TactiDex provides a comprehensive dataset that elegantly aligns whole-hand tactile signals with multi-granularity kinematic and object states, coupled with standardized evaluation metrics. Building upon this data paradigm, we propose a tactile-driven transfer framework that effectively translates human demonstrations into physically plausible robotic execution. We introduce TactiSkill, a framework built upon a novel tri-component tactile reward that innovatively uses tactile signals as structured supervision. This reward unifies guidance, human-like alignment, and contact constraints into a single objective. Through comprehensive experiments on both single and bimanual tasks, we demonstrate that TactiSkill achieves superior performance in manipulation success and physical realism. This work lays a crucial foundation for advancing tactile-aware dexterous manipulation. Our project page at https://tactidex.github.io/.

AI.tldr: TactiDex is a tactile-guided benchmark and dataset for human-to-robot dexterous manipulation transfer, paired with TactiSkill—a framework using a tri-component tactile reward—to achieve contact-level human-likeness beyond kinematic imitation, with superior success and physical realism demonstrated on single and bimanual tasks.
AI.motivation: Current human-to-robot dexterous transfer pipelines rely on kinematic trajectories, resulting in motion imitation without physically grounded interaction. Tactile feedback—fundamental to hand-object interaction for contact formation, force regulation, and stable manipulation—is neglected, preventing true human-like dexterous manipulation.
AI.method: TactiDex provides a dataset aligning whole-hand tactile signals with multi-granularity kinematic and object states, plus standardized metrics. TactiSkill uses a tri-component tactile reward unifying guidance, human-like alignment, and contact constraints as structured supervision for physically plausible robotic execution.
AI.result: TactiSkill achieves superior performance in manipulation success and physical realism on both single and bimanual tasks.
AI.conclusion: This work lays a crucial foundation for advancing tactile-aware dexterous manipulation, moving beyond kinematic mimicry toward contact-level human-likeness.

title: ARCANA: A Reflective Multi-Agent Program Synthesis Framework for ARC-AGI-2 Reasoning
summary: We present ARCANA, a collaborative multi agent framework for solving ARC AGI 2 tasks under strict test time and hardware constraints. ARCANA decomposes each task into iterative perception, hypothesis generation, symbolic execution, and reflective refinement. A perceptual grounding agent builds object centric scene graphs from raw grids, a latent program policy proposes diverse DSL programs, a symbolic executor verifies candidates on demonstrations, and a reflective agent synthesizes failure driven feedback for the next turn. These agents communicate through a shared differentiable blackboard and are scheduled by a learned meta controller. The design combines structured program search with adaptive multi turn correction, improving reasoning efficiency and solution quality on challenging abstract transformation tasks.

AI.tldr: ARCANA is a collaborative multi-agent framework that solves ARC AGI 2 tasks by combining iterative perception, hypothesis generation, symbolic execution, and reflective refinement through four specialized agents communicating via a differentiable blackboard under strict constraints.
AI.motivation: To solve challenging abstract reasoning tasks (ARC AGI 2) under strict test time and hardware constraints by decomposing the problem into structured, iterative multi-agent collaboration.
AI.method: ARCANA uses four agents: (1) a perceptual grounding agent building object-centric scene graphs, (2) a latent program policy proposing diverse DSL programs, (3) a symbolic executor verifying candidates on demonstrations, and (4) a reflective agent synthesizing failure-driven feedback. Agents communicate via a shared differentiable blackboard and are scheduled by a learned meta controller.
AI.result: Improved reasoning efficiency and solution quality on abstract transformation tasks compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Combining structured program search with adaptive multi-turn correction enhances performance on abstract visual reasoning tasks under resource constraints.

title: GenVid2Robot: From Video Generation to Robot Manipulation via Rigid-Geometric Consistency
summary: Generated videos provide useful visual motion priors for robot manipulation, but their visual plausibility does not imply physical executability. A generated video usually lacks metric geometry, grasp grounding, robot kinematic feasibility, and execution-time feedback, which makes direct trajectory replay unreliable in real-world manipulation. This paper presents GenVid2Robot, a rigid-geometric consistency framework that converts generated video motion into executable real-robot manipulation trajectories. Given an initial RGB-D observation and a task instruction, GenVid2Robot samples task-relevant semantic anchors from the real first frame, tracks these anchors through generated video candidates, and verifies whether the resulting 2D motion can be explained by first-frame RGB-D anchors under a sparse relative $SE(3)$ model. In this way, generated videos are treated as uncertain visual motion hypotheses rather than direct robot demonstrations. Only geometrically consistent motion is transferred to the robot. The accepted relative motion is then applied to the real grasp-time TCP pose selected by mask-constrained grasping, producing a grasp-conditioned execution trajectory that is consistent with both the visual motion prior and the physical grasp configuration. To reduce execution mismatch caused by RGB-D noise, calibration residuals, and small contact-induced displacement, a bounded depth-compensation module corrects local depth-direction errors without assuming full online replanning. Real-robot experiments demonstrate that GenVid2Robot improves the reliability of generated-video-guided manipulation by grounding visual motion priors with sparse metric geometry, grasp constraints, robot feasibility checking, and bounded execution feedback.

AI.tldr: GenVid2Robot converts generated videos into executable robot manipulation trajectories by enforcing rigid-geometric consistency, using sparse SE(3) motion verification, mask-constrained grasping, and bounded depth compensation to filter visually plausible but physically infeasible motion.
AI.motivation: Generated videos offer useful visual motion priors for robot manipulation, but their visual plausibility does not guarantee physical executability due to lack of metric geometry, grasp grounding, kinematic feasibility, and execution-time feedback, making direct trajectory replay unreliable.
AI.method: GenVid2Robot samples task-relevant semantic anchors from the first RGB-D frame, tracks them through generated video candidates, and checks if the 2D motion is explainable by first-frame RGB-D anchors under a sparse relative SE(3) model. Only geometrically consistent motion is transferred; accepted relative motion is applied to a real grasp-time TCP pose from mask-constrained grasping. A bounded depth-compensation module corrects local depth-direction errors from noise and calibration residuals.
AI.result: Real-robot experiments show that GenVid2Robot improves the reliability of generated-video-guided manipulation by grounding visual motion priors with sparse metric geometry, grasp constraints, robot feasibility checking, and bounded execution feedback.
AI.conclusion: Treating generated videos as uncertain visual motion hypotheses rather than direct demonstrations, and enforcing rigid-geometric consistency, enables more reliable translation of video motion priors to executable real-robot trajectories.

title: Neuro-Agentic Control: A Deep Learning-based LLM-Powered Agentic AI Framework for Controlling Security Controls
summary: Cyberattacks on operational technology are increasingly causing costly downtime and physical damage, exposing the limitations of traditional rule-based monitoring in industrial IoT environments. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have strong semantic reasoning abilities to assist in decision support, their hallucinatory nature presents unacceptable safety liabilities for closed-loop control. This paper introduces a neuro-agentic control framework, a novel architecture that couples an LLM-based planner (i.e., such as Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite) with a pre-trained Time-Series Foundation Model (TimesFM), to achieve physics-grounded autonomous defense. The paper introduces a ``Counterfactual Physics Injection'' mechanism that simulates the impact of LLM-proposed interventions within the numerical latent space of the foundation model before actuation, while allowing the system to reject hallucinatory or unsafe actions. Evaluated on an industrial dataset (e.g., the Secure Water Treatment (SWaT)) in the context of stochastic attack scenarios, the framework exhibited better performance compared to LSTM and TCN baselines. The Neuro-Agentic Loop prevented five breaches (33.3%) below the threshold versus LSTM (26.7%) and TCN (13.3%), with zero physically invalid (hallucinated) actions executed. These results demonstrate the efficacy of using foundation models as deterministic ``Sentinels'' to safeguard agentic AI in critical infrastructure.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a neuro-agentic control framework that couples an LLM-based planner with a Time-Series Foundation Model (TimesFM), using a "Counterfactual Physics Injection" mechanism to reject hallucinated/unsafe actions before actuation. Evaluated on SWaT dataset under stochastic attacks, it outperformed LSTM and TCN baselines, preventing 33.3% of breaches with zero physically invalid actions executed.
AI.motivation: Cyberattacks on operational technology are causing costly downtime and physical damage, and traditional rule-based monitoring is insufficient in industrial IoT environments. LLMs offer semantic reasoning for decision support but their hallucinatory nature poses unacceptable safety risks for closed-loop control in critical infrastructure.
AI.method: A neuro-agentic control framework coupling an LLM-based planner (Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite) with a pre-trained Time-Series Foundation Model (TimesFM). A "Counterfactual Physics Injection" mechanism simulates LLM-proposed interventions in the foundation model's numerical latent space before actuation, enabling rejection of hallucinatory or unsafe actions.
AI.result: On the SWaT dataset under stochastic attack scenarios, the framework outperformed LSTM and TCN baselines. The Neuro-Agentic Loop prevented five breaches (33.3%) below threshold vs LSTM (26.7%) and TCN (13.3%), with zero physically invalid (hallucinated) actions executed.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the efficacy of using foundation models as deterministic "Sentinels" to safeguard agentic AI in critical infrastructure, enabling physics-grounded autonomous defense while eliminating hallucinated actions.

title: Empirical Pedestrian Safety Assessment in a Mobile Robot Using a Predictive Social Force Model
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 2 Tables, IEEE/ASME International Conference on Advanced Intelligent Mechatronics
summary: Mobile robots are going to share the sidewalks with pedestrians. They must ensure their objective safety and respect the walkers' subjective safety/comfort. Computationally efficient Social Force Models (SFM) present interpretable solutions for real-time robot navigation in dynamic crowds. Recent explorations of Projected Time-to-collision (PTTC) integration into SFM variants, for example, PTTC-based SFM (TSFM), improve safety metrics. But the effect of predictive variants is unclear. We introduce Predictive SFM (PSFM) and Predictive TSFM (PTSFM) by integrating predicted social force vectors over a finite time horizon. The paper implements SFM, TSFM, PSFM, and PTSFM on a nonholonomic mobile robot and performs experimental trials with volunteers attending a facing scenario. We systematically study objective and subjective safety across the variants. Minimum PTTC, average speed, minimum distance, lateral distance, and the maximum trajectory curvature benchmark the objective safety. Likert scale post-interaction surveys assess subjective safety by marking comfort, smoothness, distance appropriateness, and speed suitability. We confirm that PTTC integration improves safety metrics. The prediction contribution is limited and occasionally visible in some of the sub-metrics. Some participants perceive smoother movements and safer speed behavior with predictive methods, but Mann-Whitney tests reveal no significant differences in subjective ratings. Therefore, PTTC-based navigation enhances safety, whereas the formulated prediction offers limited additional benefits in single-pedestrian scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Predictive SFM (PSFM) and Predictive TSFM (PTSFM) variants that integrate predicted social force vectors over a finite time horizon, and evaluates them against SFM and TSFM on a nonholonomic robot in facing scenarios with volunteers. PTTC integration improves objective safety metrics, but prediction offers only limited additional benefits in single-pedestrian scenarios, with no significant differences in subjective safety ratings.
AI.motivation: Mobile robots sharing sidewalks with pedestrians must ensure both objective safety and subjective comfort. Previous PTTC-based SFM (TSFM) improved safety, but the effect of predictive variants remained unclear, motivating the need for systematic investigation.
AI.method: Proposed Predictive SFM (PSFM) and Predictive TSFM (PTSFM) by integrating predicted social force vectors over a finite time horizon. Implemented SFM, TSFM, PSFM, and PTSFM on a nonholonomic mobile robot and conducted experimental trials with volunteers in a facing scenario. Evaluated objective safety via minimum PTTC, average speed, minimum distance, lateral distance, and maximum trajectory curvature; assessed subjective safety via Likert-scale surveys on comfort, smoothness, distance, and speed, with Mann-Whitney tests for significance.
AI.result: PTTC integration improved objective safety metrics. Prediction contribution was limited and occasionally visible in some sub-metrics. Some participants perceived smoother movements and safer speed behavior with predictive methods, but Mann-Whitney tests showed no significant differences in subjective ratings.
AI.conclusion: PTTC-based navigation enhances safety, while the formulated prediction offers limited additional benefits in single-pedestrian scenarios.

title: L-MAD: A Systematic Evaluation of Multi-Agent Debate Structures in Legal Reasoning
comment: Outstanding paper in the AI4Law Workshop at ICML 2026
summary: While multi-agent debate (MAD) frameworks have shown significant potential in general reasoning, their effectiveness in highly structured, knowledge-heavy legal domains remains under-explored. In this work, we introduce the Legal Multi-Agent Debate (L-MAD) framework to systematically evaluate different debate structures and aggregation methods within Legal Textual Entailment. By assigning distinct expert personas to multiple agents, L-MAD improves upon strong single-agent baselines by up to 8\%. Furthermore, analyzing how debate scales reveals a clear trade-off: increasing the agent population reduces inconsistency and improves accuracy, whereas extending discussion rounds induces a detrimental \textit{over-deliberation drift} where agents reinforce each other's mistakes. Ultimately, our findings outline the practical boundaries and safety margins of deploying collaborative multi-agent systems in high-stakes legal reasoning environments.

AI.tldr: L-MAD framework improves legal textual entailment reasoning through multi-agent debate, achieving up to 8% improvement over single-agent baselines, but reveals trade-offs where more agents improve accuracy while more discussion rounds cause over-deliberation drift.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent debate frameworks have shown promise in general reasoning tasks, but their effectiveness in highly structured, knowledge-heavy legal domains remains unexplored.
AI.method: Introduces the Legal Multi-Agent Debate (L-MAD) framework that assigns distinct expert personas to multiple agents, systematically evaluating different debate structures and aggregation methods within Legal Textual Entailment.
AI.result: L-MAD improves upon strong single-agent baselines by up to 8%. Increasing agent population reduces inconsistency and improves accuracy, while extending discussion rounds induces over-deliberation drift where agents reinforce each other's mistakes.
AI.conclusion: The findings outline practical boundaries and safety margins for deploying collaborative multi-agent systems in high-stakes legal reasoning environments.

title: Tactile and Vision Conditioned Contact-Centric Control for Whole-Arm Manipulation
summary: Whole-arm manipulation involves direct contact with the environment while the robot completes a task by distributing contact across multiple links as contacts form, slide, and break. This setting breaks common implicit assumptions in many learning-based manipulation pipelines: arm configuration tightly couples motion and contact forces, contact state is partially observed under occlusion, and purely learned rollouts can become physically inconsistent under distribution shift because many multi-link contact configurations are sparsely represented in the data. To address this, we propose TACTIC (Tactile and Vision Conditioned Contact-Centric Control), a receding-horizon controller for whole-arm manipulation. TACTIC uses a contact-centric hybrid predictive model that combines RGB-D, distributed tactile sensing, and a compact 2D proximity representation. The model couples a learned, action-conditioned latent dynamics model with analytical kinematics through contact Jacobians, enabling rollouts of future contact configurations and interaction forces. TACTIC integrates these rollouts into a sampling-based MPC planner with contact-aware action sampling: contact Jacobian-based projections steer sampled action sequences toward force-modulating directions, and objectives defined over predicted proximity and interaction forces trade task progress against whole-arm force regulation. We evaluate TACTIC in simulation against state-of-the-art model-based and model-free methods, and perform ablations that isolate the contribution of each design choice. TACTIC consistently outperforms other methods. We further demonstrate real-world performance on a robot with distributed tactile sensing across three whole-arm manipulation tasks that require multi-contact trajectories: turning over and repositioning a manikin, and goal-reaching in a 3D dynamic maze. Website: https://emprise.cs.cornell.edu/tactic

AI.tldr: TACTIC is a receding-horizon controller for whole-arm manipulation that combines RGB-D, tactile, and proximity sensing with a hybrid predictive model (learned latent dynamics + analytical contact Jacobians) to plan contact-aware actions via sampling-based MPC, outperforming baselines in simulation and real-world multi-contact tasks.
AI.motivation: Whole-arm manipulation involves multi-link contacts that break common assumptions in learning-based pipelines: tight coupling between arm configuration and contact forces, partially observed contact state under occlusion, and sparse representation of multi-link contact configurations causing distribution shift in purely learned rollouts.
AI.method: TACTIC uses a contact-centric hybrid predictive model combining RGB-D, distributed tactile sensing, and 2D proximity representations. It couples a learned action-conditioned latent dynamics model with analytical kinematics via contact Jacobians. A sampling-based MPC planner uses contact Jacobian-based projections for contact-aware action sampling and objectives trading task progress against whole-arm force regulation.
AI.result: TACTIC consistently outperforms state-of-the-art model-based and model-free methods in simulation, with ablations validating each design choice. Real-world experiments on three whole-arm manipulation tasks (turning/repositioning a manikin, goal-reaching in a 3D dynamic maze) demonstrate practical multi-contact trajectory capability.
AI.conclusion: Integrating tactile and vision sensing with a hybrid model that combines learned dynamics and analytical contact kinematics enables effective whole-arm manipulation under multi-contact conditions, outperforming purely learned or purely model-based approaches.

title: MedRealMM: A Real-World Multimodal Benchmark for Chinese Online Medical Consultation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in online medical consultation, yet existing benchmarks remain poorly aligned with real clinical practice. Many rely on synthetic conversations or patient simulators, omit patient-uploaded medical images, or evaluate open-ended clinical responses using multiple-choice or lexical-overlap metrics that poorly reflect clinical quality. We introduce \textbf{MedRealMM}, a large-scale benchmark for multimodal online medical consultation built from de-identified patient-doctor interactions collected from a nationwide Chinese internet hospital. MedRealMM uses a Multimodal Clinical Challenge Point (MCCP) extraction framework to identify clinically demanding moments in authentic consultation trajectories and converts each into a standardized next-response generation task while preserving the preceding text-image context. Each instance is paired with a case-specific rubric refined by physicians that rewards clinically desirable behaviors and penalizes unsafe, unsupported, or contradictory responses. The current release contains 5,620 real-world multimodal cases spanning 64 clinical departments. We evaluate 19 general-purpose and medical-specialized LLMs, including text-only and multimodal systems. Our results show that image information is critical for reliable clinical performance and that current frontier models remain below the online physician response. Although some frontier models satisfy as many or more positive clinical criteria than physicians, they trigger more negative criteria, indicating that safety-sensitive error avoidance remains a central bottleneck. MedRealMM offers a realistic and reproducible benchmark for evaluating multimodal medical reasoning in real-world online consultation. The dataset will be publicly available on Hugging Face at https://huggingface.co/datasets/jdh-algo/MedRealMM.

AI.tldr: MedRealMM is a large-scale benchmark for multimodal online medical consultation built from 5,620 real-world patient-doctor interactions across 64 clinical departments, using a Multimodal Clinical Challenge Point (MCCP) framework to extract clinically demanding moments and evaluate LLMs on next-response generation with case-specific rubrics. Results show that image information is critical for clinical performance and current frontier models, while matching physicians on positive criteria, trigger more negative (safety) criteria.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLMs in online medical consultation are poorly aligned with real clinical practice: they rely on synthetic conversations, omit patient-uploaded medical images, and use multiple-choice or lexical-overlap metrics that fail to reflect true clinical quality.
AI.method: The authors built MedRealMM from de-identified patient-doctor interactions from a nationwide Chinese internet hospital. They propose a Multimodal Clinical Challenge Point (MCCP) extraction framework to identify clinically demanding moments in consultation trajectories and convert each into a standardized next-response generation task preserving preceding text-image context. Each instance is paired with a case-specific rubric refined by physicians that rewards clinically desirable behaviors and penalizes unsafe, unsupported, or contradictory responses.
AI.result: Evaluation of 19 LLMs (general-purpose and medical-specialized, text-only and multimodal) shows: (1) image information is critical for reliable clinical performance; (2) current frontier models remain below the level of online physician responses; (3) although some frontier models satisfy as many or more positive clinical criteria than physicians, they trigger more negative criteria, indicating safety-sensitive error avoidance remains a central bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: MedRealMM offers a realistic and reproducible benchmark for evaluating multimodal medical reasoning in real-world online consultation, highlighting that safety-sensitive error avoidance is the primary limitation of current LLMs in this domain.

title: Implicit-Behavior Coordination from Unlabeled Sub-Task Demonstrations for Rearrangement Tasks
summary: Long-horizon robotic rearrangement tasks are often treated as skill sequencing problems, requiring predefined skills, skill labels, or boundaries, and task-specific switching logic. Although effective, such explicit skill abstractions can become difficult to scale as the number of behaviors and the task horizon increase. We instead formulate rearrangement as implicit-behavior coordination from unlabeled sub-task demonstrations, where skill-like behaviors are learned directly from mixed behavior data and coordinated through value-guided action selection. Experiments in Habitat rearrangement tasks support this formulation in three ways. First, our method outperforms task-specific imitation baselines on more complex rearrangement tasks and approaches an oracle-planner baseline with behavior-cloned skills, while using no oracle task plan or skill-labeled full-task demonstrations. Second, ablations show that reliable critic-guided candidate selection is essential for coordinating multi-modal behaviors. Third, scaling experiments show that the method handles larger behavior repertoires and maintains stronger performance than task-specific imitation baselines as chained targets extend the horizon. These results suggest that explicit skill abstraction is not a prerequisite for long-horizon rearrangement, and that implicit-behavior coordination offers a promising data-driven alternative to explicit skill-based pipelines.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes implicit-behavior coordination for long-horizon robotic rearrangement, where skills are learned directly from unlabeled sub-task demonstrations and coordinated via value-guided action selection, eliminating the need for explicit skill abstractions, skill labels, and task-specific switching logic.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for long-horizon robotic rearrangement rely on explicit skill abstractions (predefined skills, skill labels, boundaries, and task-specific switching logic), which become difficult to scale as the number of behaviors and task horizon increase.
AI.method: The method learns skill-like behaviors directly from mixed, unlabeled sub-task demonstration data and coordinates them through value-guided action selection, formulating rearrangement as implicit-behavior coordination without explicit skill decomposition.
AI.result: The method outperforms task-specific imitation baselines on complex rearrangement tasks and approaches oracle-planner baselines with behavior-cloned skills. Ablations confirm that critic-guided candidate selection is essential, and scaling experiments show better performance than task-specific imitation baselines as task horizon increases.
AI.conclusion: Explicit skill abstraction is not a prerequisite for long-horizon rearrangement; implicit-behavior coordination provides a promising data-driven alternative to explicit skill-based pipelines.

title: KV-PRM: Efficient Process Reward Modeling via KV-Cache Transfer for Multi-Agent Test-Time Scaling
summary: Process Reward Models (PRMs) have been proven to be highly effective in guiding test-time scaling (TTS) methods, which significantly boost the capabilities of LLM-based multi-agent systems. However, existing PRMs are text-based: they re-encode the entire trajectory text from scratch. In long multi-agent rollouts, the scoring cost, growing quadratically with respect to sequence length L, creates a severe computational bottleneck, severely limiting PRMs' application in long-context scenarios. To resolve this, we introduce KV-PRM, a highly efficient process reward model that eliminates the heavy text re-encoding by directly reading the KV cache produced naturally during the LLM's generation phase. By processing a single "verify token" against the pre-existing KV cache, KV-PRM reduces the scoring cost from O(L^2) to O(L). We formally prove that the KV cache contains strictly greater information capacity than text, and is more efficient for downstream reward modeling. Empirically, across the MATH, GSM8K, and AIME benchmarks, KV-PRM matches or strictly outperforms text-PRMs under various TTS methods such as Beam Search, MCTS, and Weighted Voting, with up to a 5,000x reduction in scoring FLOPs, a 37x reduction in latency, and a 34x reduction in per-sequence memory footprint compared to text-based PRMs.

AI.tldr: KV-PRM is a process reward model that eliminates costly text re-encoding by directly leveraging the KV cache from LLM generation, reducing scoring cost from O(L²) to O(L). It matches or outperforms text-PRMs across math reasoning benchmarks with up to 5000x FLOPs reduction, 37x latency reduction, and 34x memory reduction.
AI.motivation: Existing text-based PRMs re-encode entire trajectory text from scratch, causing O(L²) computational cost that becomes a severe bottleneck for long multi-agent rollouts, limiting PRM applications in long-context scenarios.
AI.method: KV-PRM directly reads the pre-existing KV cache from the LLM's generation phase instead of re-encoding text. It processes a single "verify token" against the cached KV representations, reducing scoring complexity from quadratic to linear in sequence length.
AI.result: KV-PRM matches or strictly outperforms text-PRMs on MATH, GSM8K, and AIME benchmarks under various TTS methods (Beam Search, MCTS, Weighted Voting), while achieving up to 5000x reduction in scoring FLOPs, 37x latency reduction, and 34x memory reduction per sequence.
AI.conclusion: The KV cache contains strictly greater information capacity than text and is more efficient for downstream reward modeling. KV-PRM provides a practical solution for scaling PRM-based reasoning to long-context scenarios.

title: Validating Virtual Reality for Studying Multimodal Human-Robot Interaction in Socially Aware Robot Navigation
summary: Virtual Reality (VR) offers a flexible and controllable platform for studying human-robot interaction. Prior work has explored VR for socially aware robot navigation. However, whether VR captures the multimodal interaction dynamics observed in real-world human-robot co-navigation remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we present a VR prototype and evaluate its suitability for studying multimodal human-robot interaction (HRI) in socially aware navigation. Specifically, we investigate whether VR preserves the multimodal interaction dynamics observed in real-world human-robot co-navigation. We conducted a within-subjects study (N = 21) in which participants interacted with a PR2 mobile manipulator robot in both a motion capture equipped arena and its virtual replica in an immersive VR environment. Two common co-navigation scenarios were examined : orthogonal crossing and pass-by interactions. Participants evaluated the robot's perceived social awareness and interaction comfort, while trajectory and head-orientation data were analysed to examine behavioral responses during the interaction. Our results show that participants perceive the robot's socially aware navigation similarly in VR and in the real world. Furthermore, VR captures human interaction behaviors in ways consistent with real-world observations. These findings suggest that VR can be a reliable and flexible platform for studying richer multimodal behaviors in social navigation and HRI.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a VR prototype for studying multimodal human-robot interaction in socially aware navigation, and validates through a within-subjects study (N=21) that VR preserves real-world interaction dynamics—participants perceived robot social awareness similarly and exhibited consistent behavioral responses in both environments.
AI.motivation: Prior work has used VR for socially aware robot navigation, but whether VR captures the multimodal interaction dynamics observed in real-world human-robot co-navigation remains insufficiently understood.
AI.method: A within-subjects study (N=21) where participants interacted with a PR2 robot in both a motion capture arena and its VR replica. Two co-navigation scenarios (orthogonal crossing and pass-by) were examined using subjective evaluations (social awareness, comfort) and objective measures (trajectory, head-orientation).
AI.result: Participants perceived the robot's socially aware navigation similarly in VR and real world. VR captured human interaction behaviors consistent with real-world observations.
AI.conclusion: VR can be a reliable and flexible platform for studying richer multimodal behaviors in social navigation and HRI.

title: Scoped Verification for Reliable Long-Horizon Agentic Context Evolution under Distribution Shift
summary: Deployed LLM agents rely on agentic context, the model-external textual control content assembled by an operational harness. In this work, the mutable component of that context is a persistent system-level instruction that is updated from operational experience while the model, tools, and harness remain fixed. Over long evolution horizons, flat-text maintenance makes verification increasingly difficult as accumulated instructions grow and interact. We propose Graph-Regularized Agentic Context Evolution (GRACE), which maintains the persistent instruction component as a typed semantic graph and validates proposed updates within the local typed neighborhoods of modified nodes. Accepted graph updates are reconstructed as incremental edits to the textual instruction checkpoint used at deployment. We evaluate GRACE within a fixed telecom agent harness derived from $τ^2$-bench under a controlled distribution-shift protocol. Across five independent replications, GRACE improves strict reliability, measured by pass^3, from the Gemini 2.5 Flash zero-shot value of 0.091 to 0.673$\pm$0.136 at the final checkpoint. This exceeds a Gemini 3.1 Pro zero-shot reference of 0.242 on the same held-out set, while the flat-text HCE baseline finishes at 0.191$\pm$0.051. These results identify two requirements for reliable long-horizon context evolution, a structural substrate that makes verification local and a consolidation mechanism that keeps accumulated instruction content usable.

AI.tldr: GRACE replaces flat-text persistent instructions with a typed semantic graph for LLM agent context evolution, enabling local verification of updates through typed neighborhood validation. Applied to a telecom agent task, it boosts pass^3 from 0.091 (zero-shot) to 0.673±0.136, outperforming flat-text baselines (0.191±0.051) and Gemini 3.1 Pro zero-shot (0.242).
AI.motivation: Deployed LLM agents rely on persistent system-level instructions that accumulate over long evolution horizons. Flat-text maintenance of these instructions makes verification increasingly difficult as instructions grow and interact, creating a need for a more structured approach to context evolution.
AI.method: GRACE maintains the persistent instruction component as a typed semantic graph, validates proposed updates within local typed neighborhoods of modified nodes, and reconstructs accepted graph updates as incremental edits to the textual instruction checkpoint used at deployment.
AI.result: GRACE improved pass^3 from 0.091 (Gemini 2.5 Flash zero-shot) to 0.673±0.136 at final checkpoint, exceeding Gemini 3.1 Pro zero-shot (0.242) and flat-text HCE baseline (0.191±0.051) across five independent replications on a telecom agent task with controlled distribution shift.
AI.conclusion: Two requirements for reliable long-horizon context evolution are identified: a structural substrate that makes verification local, and a consolidation mechanism that keeps accumulated instruction content usable.

title: Robot Trajectron V3: A Probabilistic Shared Control Framework for SE(3) Manipulation
summary: We aim to address the challenge of teleoperating robotic arms for high-degree-of-freedom (high-DoF) manipulation tasks, which is cognitively demanding and error-prone, particularly when relying on low-bandwidth interfaces. We propose Robot Trajectron V3 (RT-V3), a probabilistic shared control framework designed for $SE(3)$ grasping tasks. RT-V3 formulates shared control as Bayesian inference by learning a prior over user intent and combining it with real-time user commands to estimate the posterior intent distribution. The prior models user intent as a distribution over future trajectories conditioned on past robot dynamics and visual scene context. The intent prior is parameterized by a transformer-based conditional generative model that reasons over point clouds and candidate grasp poses, together with a factorized translation-rotation representation that improves learning efficiency in high-dimensional action spaces. During execution, RT-V3 continuously estimates the posterior distribution over future trajectories by combining the learned intent prior with a user-command likelihood derived from the observed control input, enabling continuous intent refinement and shared assistance. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that RT-V3 achieves high accuracy in trajectory prediction and competitive performance in reactive planning. Furthermore, real-world user studies indicate that RT-V3 significantly outperforms baseline methods in terms of success rate and efficiency, while substantially reducing the user's physical and mental workload.

AI.tldr: RT-V3 is a probabilistic shared control framework for teleoperated robotic arm grasping that uses transformer-based intent priors and Bayesian inference to reduce cognitive load and improve task success rate and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Teleoperating high-DoF robotic arms for manipulation tasks is cognitively demanding and error-prone, especially with low-bandwidth interfaces. Existing approaches lack efficient probabilistic intent inference to alleviate user burden.
AI.method: RT-V3 formulates shared control as Bayesian inference: a transformer-based conditional generative model learns a prior over user intent (future trajectories) conditioned on past robot dynamics and point cloud scene context, using a factorized translation-rotation representation. During execution, this prior is combined with real-time user commands via a likelihood model to estimate the posterior intent distribution continuously.
AI.result: High accuracy in trajectory prediction and competitive reactive planning performance. Real-world user studies show significantly higher success rate and efficiency, with substantially reduced physical and mental workload compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Probabilistic shared control with learned intent priors effectively reduces cognitive burden and improves teleoperation performance for high-DoF grasping tasks.

title: Toward Auditable AI Scientists: A Hypothesis Evolution Protocol for LLM Agents
