summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to play a central role in AI-driven scientific discovery. Equipped with broad knowledge, flexible reasoning, and tool use, they have the potential to autonomously explore and solve scientific problems by repeatedly proposing hypotheses, testing them, and revising their beliefs in the light of the evidence. In current agents, however, these hypotheses, tests, and belief updates are buried in unstructured logs, and no mechanism lets the agent or the human researcher audit that process. Here we propose the Hypothesis Evolution Protocol (HEP), an agent harness that provides hypothesis generation, evaluation, and evolution as explicit, auditable operations. On materials-science research tasks, a HEP-equipped agent operates the hypothesis--test--evidence--belief cycle that planning-style agents lack, generalizes across research questions, and exploits the protocol more fully as the base LLM becomes more capable. These results mark a step toward auditable AI scientists, whose scientific reasoning can be inspected, verified, and built upon.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Hypothesis Evolution Protocol (HEP), an agent harness that makes hypothesis generation, testing, and belief updating explicit and auditable in LLM-based scientific discovery agents, demonstrating improved performance on materials-science tasks.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents for scientific discovery lack explicit mechanisms for hypothesis generation, testing, and belief revision; their reasoning processes are buried in unstructured logs, preventing both the agent and human researchers from auditing the scientific process.
AI.method: The authors design the Hypothesis Evolution Protocol (HEP), an agent harness that structures hypothesis generation, evaluation, and evolution as explicit, auditable operations, enabling a clear hypothesis-test-evidence-belief cycle.
AI.result: On materials-science research tasks, HEP-equipped agents outperform planning-style agents, generalize across different research questions, and exploit the protocol more fully as the base LLM capability increases.
AI.conclusion: HEP represents a step toward auditable AI scientists whose scientific reasoning can be inspected, verified, and built upon by human researchers.

title: Differential Analysis of Multispectral Images for Terrain Identification
summary: Reliable terrain understanding is a prerequisite for autonomous robot navigation. Yet, the widespread RGB-based perception can fail under low illumination, shadows, and material ambiguities. In this work we propose DRIFT, a lightweight multispectral framework that combines raw spectral bands and illumination-tolerant band-ratio representations through a dual-stream residual architecture and a differential fusion branch. Band ratios attenuate multiplicative acquisition effects (illumination/sensor gains), while the differential fusion explicitly highlights discrepancies between absolute-band and ratio-derived cues, which improves the robustness to noisy or partially unreliable spectral measurements. In the paper (i) we evaluate DRIFT on a new oil-on-soil multispectral dataset acquired using a MicaSense RedEdge-P camera mounted on an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle, and (ii) we provide an additional controlled study on water-on-grass under varying illumination and thermal perturbations (hot/cold water) to analyze NIR-sensitive effects. DRIFT consistently improves over strong baselines, while remaining compatible with edge deployment.

AI.tldr: DRIFT is a lightweight multispectral framework for terrain understanding that combines raw spectral bands and band-ratio representations via a dual-stream residual architecture with differential fusion, achieving robust performance under challenging illumination and material conditions while being edge-deployable.
AI.motivation: RGB-based perception for autonomous robot navigation fails under low illumination, shadows, and material ambiguities, motivating the need for a more robust multispectral approach.
AI.method: DRIFT uses a dual-stream residual architecture with differential fusion: one stream processes raw spectral bands, the other processes illumination-tolerant band-ratio representations, and the differential fusion branch highlights discrepancies between absolute-band and ratio-derived cues to improve robustness to noisy spectral measurements.
AI.result: DRIFT consistently outperforms strong baselines on a new oil-on-soil multispectral UAV dataset and a controlled water-on-grass study under varying illumination and thermal perturbations, while remaining compatible with edge deployment.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multispectral framework provides reliable terrain understanding for autonomous navigation, particularly under challenging lighting and material conditions, with practical edge-deployment feasibility.

title: OpenProver: Agentic and Interactive Theorem Proving with Lean 4
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at the 19th Conference on Intelligent Computer Mathematics (CICM 2026)
summary:
In this system paper, we present OpenProver, an open-source system for LLM-driven automated theorem proving (ATP) with integrated Lean 4 formal verification. OpenProver integrates a Planner-Worker-Verifier architecture inspired by recent ATP agentic systems such as Aletheia. A Planner agent maintains a compact Whiteboard scratchpad and an unbounded Repository of intermediate findings, and decomposes mathematical work into parallel Workers.
  OpenProver is fully open-source, offers reproducible evaluation through automatic formal verification of generated proofs, and provides an interactive terminal interface for human-guided proof search. In interactive mode, OpenProver allows the human operator to monitor and steer the proof search process, motivated by the established human-AI synergy in interactive code generation.
  To showcase the potential for quantitative ablation experiments enabled by automatic formal verification, we evaluate OpenProver on ProofNet and compare it with a simple baseline. OpenProver is publicly available at https://github.com/kripner/OpenProver.

AI.tldr: OpenProver is an open-source system for LLM-driven automated theorem proving with Lean 4 verification, featuring a Planner-Worker-Verifier architecture, interactive human-guided mode, and reproducible evaluation.
AI.motivation: To provide an open-source, reproducible, and interactive system for LLM-based automated theorem proving that supports human-AI synergy and enables quantitative ablation studies.
AI.method: Planner-Worker-Verifier architecture: Planner maintains a compact Whiteboard scratchpad and unbounded Repository of intermediate findings, decomposing mathematical work into parallel Workers, with automatic formal verification in Lean 4 and optional interactive terminal interface for human guidance.
AI.result: Evaluated on ProofNet against a simple baseline, demonstrating the potential for quantitative ablation experiments enabled by automatic formal verification.
AI.conclusion: OpenProver advances open-source ATP by combining LLM-driven search with Lean 4 verification, human interaction, and reproducible evaluation.

title: Effects of Robotic Touch on Older Users During Walking Guidance by a Humanoid Robot
summary: The shortage of healthcare staff is a challenge in geriatric care. To address this, robots can be integrated into care settings to provide assistance and emotional support. A promising application is walking guidance, particularly benefiting older adults as navigation skills deteriorate with aging. As walking guidance involves direct contact, the aim of this study is to understand how older adults perceive and respond to different touch modes during guided walking. 24 older adults (68 - 88 yrs.) walked four times a ten-meter trajectory guided by the robot TIAGo Pro in four contact conditions: no physical contact (NC); physical contact through holding the robot's wrist with the hand (HH); physical interaction through linking arms with the robot (LA); and physical contact through resting the forearm on the robots forearm (FC). A multimodal assessment approach included electrocardiogram, electrodermal activity, contact force, distance to robot, and questionnaires. Physiological results reveal a slight increase in stress levels during robot interaction. Behavioural and subjective measures, however, show overall acceptance of robotic touch. The two conditions corresponding to larger interaction forces (HH and FC) were associated with lower relative distances between participant and robot, indicating a higher trust and confidence. Questionnaire responses supported these findings, evidencing greater perceived safety, trust and comfort in these conditions. This study provides insights for the design of robotic walking guidance assistance, indicating that gentle, stable touch is preferred by older adults in comparison to contactless interaction.

AI.tldr: This study investigated how 24 older adults (68-88 yrs) perceive different touch modes during robot-guided walking using TIAGo Pro. Four contact conditions were tested: no contact, holding wrist, linking arms, and forearm contact. Results showed that physical contact conditions (especially holding wrist and forearm contact) led to higher trust, perceived safety, and comfort, though physiological measures indicated slight stress increases.
AI.motivation: To address healthcare staff shortages in geriatric care by integrating robots for walking guidance, and to understand how older adults perceive and respond to different touch modes during guided walking, as navigation skills deteriorate with aging.
AI.method: 24 older adults (68-88 yrs) walked a ten-meter trajectory guided by robot TIAGo Pro under four conditions: no contact (NC), holding robot's wrist (HH), linking arms (LA), and forearm contact (FC). Multimodal assessment included ECG, electrodermal activity, contact force, distance to robot, and questionnaires.
AI.result: Physiological results showed slight stress increase during robot interaction. Behavioral and subjective measures indicated overall acceptance of robotic touch. Conditions with larger interaction forces (HH and FC) were associated with lower relative distances (higher trust/confidence) and greater perceived safety, trust, and comfort.
AI.conclusion: Gentle, stable touch is preferred by older adults over contactless interaction during robotic walking guidance, providing design insights for robotic assistance in geriatric care.

title: LongMedBench: Benchmarking Medical Agents for Long-Horizon Clinical Decision-Making
comment: Submitted manuscript prior to peer review in MICCAI 2026
summary: In this work, we introduce LongMedBench, a real-world EHR-based benchmark for long-horizon clinical decision-making. Prior evaluations of LLM-based medical agents have largely emphasized short-context knowledge QA and tool use. However, real-world medical care is inherently longitudinal, and clinicians must aggregate evidence across repeated visits, tests, and evolving treatments. Therefore, long-horizon interaction is essential for realistic assessment. LongMedBench is constructed via a reproducible pipeline that integrates MIMIC-IV admission records and clinical notes into time-series event streams and long-context memory datasets, enabling long-horizon, multi-session interactions between agents and a clinical environment. It comprises 335 patients, with 19.72 inpatient visits per patient on average and 44.91 medical events per visit. Guided by the long-horizon decision process, we propose an evaluation taxonomy with three suites: fact-based QA, temporal reasoning, and long-horizon decision-making. This taxonomy measures how agents understand and leverage historical patient information over extended horizons. Our experiments show that while recent LLMs can make good use of explicit timestamps, they have challenges in implicit time inference; The RAG and agent memory system can improve the performance of information retrieval tasks, but the performance of decision-making tasks is highly dependent on the model's immediate context.

AI.tldr: LongMedBench is a benchmark for evaluating LLM-based medical agents on long-horizon clinical decision-making, using real EHR data from MIMIC-IV with 335 patients, ~20 visits and ~45 events per visit. It introduces three evaluation suites (fact-based QA, temporal reasoning, long-horizon decision-making). Findings show LLMs handle explicit timestamps well but struggle with implicit time inference; RAG/agent memory helps retrieval but decision-making depends on immediate context.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM medical agent evaluations focus on short-context QA and tool use, ignoring the longitudinal, multi-visit nature of real clinical care. There is no benchmark that captures long-horizon, multi-session decision-making where agents must aggregate evidence across repeated visits and evolving treatments.
AI.method: A reproducible pipeline integrates MIMIC-IV admission records and clinical notes into time-series event streams and long-context memory datasets, enabling multi-session interactions. The benchmark includes 335 patients with 19.72 inpatient visits and 44.91 medical events per patient on average. An evaluation taxonomy with three suites is proposed: fact-based QA, temporal reasoning, and long-horizon decision-making.
AI.result: Recent LLMs make good use of explicit timestamps but struggle with implicit time inference. RAG and agent memory systems improve information retrieval tasks, but decision-making task performance is highly dependent on the model's immediate context.
AI.conclusion: Long-horizon interaction is essential for realistic assessment of medical AI agents. Current LLMs have significant limitations in implicit temporal reasoning and context-dependent decision-making, highlighting the need for better long-context understanding in clinical AI systems.

title: PhysV2A: Reachability-Gated and Semantic-Mask-Constrained Feasibility Completion for Video-to-Robot Manipulation
summary: Video-based manipulation provides object-centric motion priors from human demonstrations, generated videos, or RGB-D observations, but such priors are typically embodiment-agnostic and cannot be directly executed by a specific robot. This paper presents \textbf{PhysV2A}, a reachability-gated and semantic-mask-constrained feasibility-completion framework for converting video-derived 6D object motion into robot-executable manipulation trajectories. The key idea is to treat grasp feasibility as trajectory-conditioned rather than local: each RGB-D-generated 6-DoF grasp candidate is rigidly coupled with the recovered object motion to form a grasp-conditioned TCP trajectory hypothesis. PhysV2A then performs hierarchical reachability-gated selection, where infeasible grasp--trajectory pairs are rejected by robot-centric kinematic checks and surviving candidates are ranked by downstream execution suitability. For the selected reachable trajectory, a VLM-assisted and rule-validated S-Mask identifies task-critical and relaxable Cartesian components, enabling semantic-mask-constrained manipulability refinement through redundancy-first optimization and bounded Cartesian relaxation. Real-robot experiments on four tabletop manipulation tasks show that PhysV2A improves task success over representative video-prior and IK-only baselines, reduces kinematic-feasibility failures, and produces better-conditioned trajectories with bounded semantic deviations.

AI.tldr: PhysV2A converts video-derived 6D object motion into robot-executable trajectories via reachability-gated grasp selection and semantic-mask-constrained feasibility refinement.
AI.motivation: Video-based manipulation provides embodiment-agnostic motion priors that cannot be directly executed by a specific robot, necessitating a method to bridge the gap between object-centric motion and robot-specific kinematic feasibility.
AI.method: PhysV2A uses grasp-conditioned TCP trajectory hypotheses (rigidly coupling 6-DoF grasp candidates with recovered object motion), hierarchical reachability-gated selection (kinematic feasibility checks + downstream suitability ranking), and semantic-mask-constrained refinement (VLM-assisted S-Mask identifying critical vs. relaxable components, redundancy-first optimization, bounded Cartesian relaxation).
AI.result: Improves task success over video-prior and IK-only baselines, reduces kinematic-feasibility failures, and produces better-conditioned trajectories with bounded semantic deviations on four tabletop manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Treating grasp feasibility as trajectory-conditioned (not local) and using semantic-mask-constrained refinement enables effective conversion of embodiment-agnostic video priors into executable robot manipulation trajectories.

title: Communication-Efficient Digital-Twin Coordination for Heterogeneous LLM Embodied Agents over Computing Power Networks
summary: Embodied agent teams powered by heterogeneous large language models (LLMs) are being widely deployed in physical artificial intelligence such as smart factories, warehouses, and service robotics. To enable collaboration among such an agent team, efficient coordination mechanisms that operate reliably under limited network resources are required. However, existing heterogeneous LLM-agent coordination frameworks that rely on multi-round natural-language-based conversations introduce three coupled challenges. First, inter-agent dialogue incurs communication overhead that grows rapidly with team size. Second, the quality of coordination is constrained by the heterogeneous capabilities of the agent team's LLMs. Third, agents may suffer from action delays due to iterative negotiation. To address these challenges, we propose LDT-Coord, a networked coordination framework built upon a lightweight digital twin (DT). Specifically, each agent independently selects its intended action and reports both the action decision and a structured temporal constraint over shared resources to the DT server, thereby decoupling coordination performance from natural-language reasoning ability. Then, DT executes a training-free, rule-based orchestrator algorithm to resolve cross-agent conflicts and returns coordination instructions to prevent such conflicts. To further reduce communication overhead, we formulate agent reporting control as a constrained partially observable Markov decision process (C-POMDP) and solve it with the PPO-Lagrangian algorithm. Simulation results show that LDT-Coord achieves a task success rate comparable to conventional coordination methods while reducing communication overhead by more than 70x and maintaining robustness under LLM heterogeneity.

AI.tldr: LDT-Coord is a lightweight digital twin-based coordination framework for heterogeneous LLM agent teams that replaces natural-language negotiation with structured action reporting and rule-based conflict resolution, achieving comparable task success rates while reducing communication overhead by 70x+ and maintaining robustness under LLM heterogeneity.
AI.motivation: Existing heterogeneous LLM-agent coordination frameworks rely on multi-round natural-language conversations, which introduce three coupled challenges: (1) communication overhead growing rapidly with team size, (2) coordination quality constrained by heterogeneous LLM capabilities, and (3) action delays from iterative negotiation.
AI.method: Proposes LDT-Coord, a networked coordination framework where (a) agents independently select actions and report both the action and structured temporal constraints to a DT server, decoupling coordination from natural-language reasoning; (b) DT executes a training-free, rule-based orchestrator to resolve conflicts; (c) agent reporting is formulated as a C-POMDP solved with PPO-Lagrangian to minimize communication overhead.
AI.result: LDT-Coord achieves task success rates comparable to conventional coordination methods while reducing communication overhead by more than 70x and maintaining robustness under LLM heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed lightweight DT-based coordination framework effectively addresses the communication overhead, capability heterogeneity, and action delay challenges in heterogeneous LLM agent teams, offering a practical solution for deploying embodied agent teams under limited network resources.

title: One-Shot Multimodal Learning from Demonstration with Force-Constrained Elastic Maps
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Accepted for publication at IROS 2026
summary: Robotic manipulation tasks often require simultaneous reasoning over motion and contact forces, yet most Learning from Demonstration (LfD) methods model only spatial trajectories and neglect force interactions with the environment. This limitation reduces robustness and can lead to unsafe or inconsistent task reproduction in force-constrained settings. We propose a novel one-shot multimodal LfD framework for the segmentation, encoding, and reproduction of force-inclusive demonstrations. First, we introduce a multimodal probabilistic segmentation method that adaptively weighs spatial and force modalities over time, enabling the automatic extraction of force-aware motion primitives. Second, we extend the elastic maps representation to incorporate external force constraints during skill encoding and formulate a convex optimization procedure for learning force-consistent trajectory models. The resulting skills reproduce both motion and contact characteristics from a single demonstration while promoting safer execution by accounting for demonstrated force profiles. We validate our approach on five real-world manipulation tasks across two distinct force-sensing configurations: wrist force sensing on a UR5e with a Robotiq 2f-85 gripper and finger force sensing on a Kinova Gen3 with an Openhand Model O gripper. Experimental results demonstrate robust multimodal segmentation, accurate force-aware reproduction, and cross-platform generality.

AI.tldr: Proposes a one-shot multimodal LfD framework that segments, encodes, and reproduces force-inclusive demonstrations by adaptively weighting spatial and force modalities for segmentation and extending elastic maps with force constraints via convex optimization, validated on five real-world tasks across two robot platforms.
AI.motivation: Existing LfD methods primarily model spatial trajectories and neglect force interactions with the environment, leading to reduced robustness and unsafe task reproduction in force-constrained settings.
AI.method: (1) Multimodal probabilistic segmentation that adaptively weights spatial and force modalities over time for automatic extraction of force-aware motion primitives; (2) Extension of elastic maps representation to incorporate external force constraints during skill encoding via convex optimization.
AI.result: Validated on five real-world manipulation tasks using two different force-sensing configurations (wrist-mounted on UR5e and finger-mounted on Kinova Gen3), achieving robust multimodal segmentation, accurate force-aware reproduction, and cross-platform generality.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables one-shot learning of force-inclusive manipulation skills, promoting safer execution by accounting for demonstrated force profiles, and generalizes across different robotic platforms and sensing modalities.

title: Fictional Worldbuilding: Multi-Agent LLM Collaboration with Hierarchical Context Compression and Iterative Review
summary: Worldbuilding, the construction of coherent fictional worlds, is a foundational task in game design and literary creation. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer new possibilities for automated content generation, but their application to worldbuilding faces three challenges: context explosion that grows linearly with the building process, the tension between creative diversity and content consistency, and the absence of automated quality assurance. This paper presents AutoWorldBuilder, a multi-agent collaborative system that addresses these challenges through five integrated components: a structured concept network with conflict detection; a DAG-based hybrid batch scheduler that groups tasks by semantic locality; a four-layer context compression mechanism achieving approximately 90% token reduction; an iterative review system with specialized Auditor agents that improves proposal pass rates from 42% to over 85%; and a skill-driven agent architecture supporting zero-code extension with differentiated temperature configuration. Two experiments across 20 diverse worldbuilding tasks, using GPT-OSS 120B and DeepSeek v3.2 as LLM backends, demonstrate a 95.0% success rate. The system generated 56-103 self-consistent concepts per world in 18-31 minutes with zero-conflict delivery. The architectural patterns validated here, including layer-as-budget compression, semantic-locality scheduling, and separation of generation and review, transfer to the broader class of knowledge-intensive, multi-agent LLM applications.

AI.tldr: AutoWorldBuilder is a multi-agent collaborative system for automated fictional worldbuilding that uses a structured concept network, DAG-based scheduling, ~90% token compression, iterative review (boosting acceptance from 42% to >85%), and skill-driven zero-code agents, achieving 95% success rate with 56-103 consistent concepts per world in 18-31 minutes with zero conflicts.
AI.motivation: LLMs face three key challenges in automated worldbuilding: context explosion growing linearly with the building process, the tension between creative diversity and content consistency, and the absence of automated quality assurance mechanisms.
AI.method: The system integrates five components: (1) a structured concept network with conflict detection; (2) a DAG-based hybrid batch scheduler grouping tasks by semantic locality; (3) a four-layer context compression mechanism achieving ~90% token reduction; (4) an iterative review system with specialized Auditor agents; and (5) a skill-driven agent architecture supporting zero-code extension with differentiated temperature configuration.
AI.result: Across 20 diverse worldbuilding tasks using GPT-OSS 120B and DeepSeek v3.2, the system achieved a 95.0% success rate, generating 56-103 self-consistent concepts per world in 18-31 minutes with zero-conflict delivery. Proposal pass rates improved from 42% to over 85%.
AI.conclusion: The architectural patterns validated—layer-as-budget compression, semantic-locality scheduling, and separation of generation and review—are transferable to the broader class of knowledge-intensive, multi-agent LLM applications.

title: DemoBridge: A Simulation-in-the-Loop Toolkit for Single-View Human Demonstration Retargeting
summary: We present DemoBridge, an toolkit that turns a single-view RGB stereo recording of a human hand demonstration into an executable, physics-validated robot-arm trajectory. Retargeting across the embodiment gap is hard. A robot arm reaches a target with a long, articulated body whose links carry far more collision volume than a hand. Solving inverse kinematics for the mapped end-effector pose often yields no collision-free solution, and a trajectory imposes this at every waypoint. A single view adds noise, leaving the demonstrated reference inaccurate. At the core of DemoBridge is a single collision-aware planner. It optimizes the whole joint trajectory at once, reasoning jointly over alternative grasp poses, whole-arm and grasped-object collision, and fidelity to the demonstrated path. A physics simulator runs in the loop. It validates each phase as it is produced and backtracks on failure, so a demonstration that cannot be reproduced as given is re-planned rather than discarded. The resulting action sequence is dynamically stable and faithful to the demonstrated manipulation. It also doubles as a ready-to-use simulation rollout for policy learning. Grasp timing is inferred automatically, and the perception backends, robot, and pipeline stages are swappable from configuration. We evaluate whole-pipeline retargeting on three real-demonstration tasks and the planner on a controlled synthetic benchmark. Our code is available at https://gitlab.kuleuven.be/u0123974/demo-bridge/ .

AI.tldr: DemoBridge is a toolkit that converts single-view RGB stereo hand demonstrations into physics-validated robot-arm trajectories using a collision-aware planner with physics-in-the-loop validation and backtracking replanning.
AI.motivation: Retargeting human hand demonstrations to robot arms is hard due to the embodiment gap: robot arms have larger collision volumes and solving IK for mapped end-effector poses often yields no collision-free solutions across trajectory waypoints, while single-view noise adds further inaccuracy.
AI.method: A single collision-aware planner optimizes the whole joint trajectory jointly over alternative grasp poses, whole-arm and grasped-object collision, and fidelity to the demonstrated path. A physics simulator runs in the loop to validate each phase and backtrack on failure, enabling replanning rather than discarding infeasible demonstrations. Grasp timing is inferred automatically, and perception backends, robot, and pipeline stages are configurable.
AI.result: Evaluated on three real-demonstration tasks for whole-pipeline retargeting and on a controlled synthetic benchmark for the planner. The system produces dynamically stable action sequences faithful to the demonstrated manipulation that double as ready-to-use simulation rollouts for policy learning.
AI.conclusion: DemoBridge successfully bridges the embodiment gap by enabling robust retargeting of hand demonstrations to robot arms through joint optimization with physics-in-the-loop validation and automated replanning on failure.

title: How Does Bayesian Causal Discovery Fail? Characterising Structural Consequences in Linear Gaussian Networks under Latent Confounding
summary: Bayesian causal discovery is widely used for its ability to quantify epistemic uncertainty over directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) through posterior inference. However, its behaviour under latent confounding remains poorly understood, as existing work typically notes that confounding breaks identifiability without characterising how the posterior distribution over DAGs responds. In this work, we analyse posterior behaviour under latent confounding in linear Gaussian causal models, focusing on additive latent confounding between exactly two observed variables. We derive a critical correlation threshold above which the score function favours graphs with a spurious edge between the confounded variables, and show that this threshold decreases with sample size -- more data lowers the correlation required for the spurious edge to be favoured. Beyond this threshold, we characterize two distinct posterior failure regimes determined by the local structure around the confounded variables. Our findings are supported by exact posterior computations on multiple graph structures, demonstrating both the predicted failure regimes.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes how latent confounding affects Bayesian causal discovery in linear Gaussian models, deriving a correlation threshold where spurious edges are favored in posterior DAG distributions, with the threshold decreasing as sample size increases.
AI.motivation: Bayesian causal discovery is widely used for quantifying epistemic uncertainty over DAGs, but its behavior under latent confounding is poorly understood. Existing work only notes that confounding breaks identifiability without characterizing how the posterior distribution responds.
AI.method: The authors analyze posterior behavior under additive latent confounding between exactly two observed variables in linear Gaussian causal models, derive a critical correlation threshold for the score function favoring spurious edges, and characterize two posterior failure regimes based on local structure around confounded variables.
AI.result: A critical correlation threshold exists above which the score function favors graphs with spurious edges between confounded variables; this threshold decreases with sample size. Two distinct posterior failure regimes are identified based on local structure around confounded variables.
AI.conclusion: Latent confounding systematically biases posterior inference in Bayesian causal discovery, with failure modes that become more pronounced with larger sample sizes, highlighting fundamental limitations of current methods.

title: How Mobile Gas Sensor Trajectories Govern Hydrogen Leak Detection: A Safety Gap in Manual Leak Inspection of Hydrogen System Components
summary: The integrity of hydrogen infrastructure relies on reliable leak detection, performed almost exclusively via manual tracer gas sniffing in electrolyzer manufacturing. Although mandated by standards, the lack of spatial probe guidance instructions leaves detection reliability entirely to operator execution, further compromised by sensor signal delays. This study quantifies how sniffer trajectory kinematics affect detection reliability at small-scale pipes and fittings, a near-field regime largely neglected by macroscopic dispersion research. Using a robotically guided test bench to eliminate operator variability, static concentration fields and dynamic trajectory passes were acquired across representative geometries under standardized leak rates (5 vol% hydrogen in nitrogen) and varying scanning velocities. Results demonstrate that scanning velocity and spatial probe orientation strongly dictate detectability. Conventional linear trajectories frequently miss leaks under dynamic conditions, causing severe false negatives. Conversely, geometry-specific routing, such as circumferential plunging paths around sealing points, maintains a high safety margin. From these observations, geometry-specific routing rules and a reduction-factor model for dynamic signal loss are derived. The findings reveal that current standard operating procedures pose a tangible safety risk. To operationalize these rules, a proof-of-concept software pipeline is presented, generating validated trajectories directly from 3D models for visualization in assistance systems.

AI.tldr: This study quantifies how sniffer trajectory kinematics (scanning velocity and probe orientation) affect hydrogen leak detection reliability in electrolyzer manufacturing, demonstrating that conventional linear trajectories cause frequent false negatives while geometry-specific routing (e.g., circumferential plunging paths) maintains high safety margins. A reduction-factor model for dynamic signal loss and a software pipeline for generating validated trajectories from 3D models are presented.
AI.motivation: Hydrogen infrastructure leak detection relies on manual tracer gas sniffing, which lacks spatial probe guidance instructions and is compromised by sensor signal delays and operator variability, yet the near-field regime of small-scale pipes and fittings remains largely neglected by macroscopic dispersion research.
AI.method: A robotically guided test bench eliminated operator variability; static concentration fields and dynamic trajectory passes were acquired across representative geometries under standardized leak rates (5 vol% H2 in N2) and varying scanning velocities.
AI.result: Scanning velocity and spatial probe orientation strongly dictate detectability. Conventional linear trajectories frequently miss leaks under dynamic conditions (severe false negatives), while geometry-specific routing like circumferential plunging paths maintains high safety margins.
AI.conclusion: Current standard operating procedures pose a tangible safety risk. Geometry-specific routing rules and a reduction-factor model for dynamic signal loss are derived; a proof-of-concept software pipeline generates validated trajectories from 3D models for visualization in assistance systems.

title: ProofCouncil: An LLM Agent for Solving Open Mathematical Problems
comment: 25 pages, 7 figures. ProofCouncil appears as System A (IMProofBench ProofCouncil) in the official FirstProof second-batch report (arXiv:2606.18119). Code and agent-building library: https://github.com/eth-sri/proof-council
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing promise in solving open problems in mathematics. However, their performance can be further improved through agentic workflows tailored to real-world mathematical practice. To this end, we introduce ProofCouncil, a mathematical agent that is designed to tackle open problems using an author-critic architecture. ProofCouncil served as a submission to the second batch of FirstProof, a challenge consisting of 10 real-world mathematical problems that agents must solve autonomously. Its submissions for 6 of the 10 problems were judged by the referees to be correct up to at most minor revisions, showing the best performance among participating teams. We also evaluate ProofCouncil on 30 open problems collected from mathematical researchers. Among the 21 solutions that received human feedback, 5 were judged completely correct, 2 more were judged promising pending final verification, and a further 8 contained useful partial progress. In this short paper, we describe the development of ProofCouncil and the agent-building library used to create it, which we release as open source to the community.

AI.tldr: ProofCouncil is a mathematical agent using an author-critic architecture that solved 6 of 10 open problems in the FirstProof challenge (best performance), and produced 5 completely correct solutions among 21 evaluated open problems from researchers.
AI.motivation: LLMs show promise in solving open math problems, but their performance can be further improved through agentic workflows tailored to real-world mathematical practice.
AI.method: Author-critic architecture where the agent generates solutions and critiques them iteratively, built using an open-source agent-building library.
AI.result: Best performance in FirstProof challenge (6/10 problems correct up to minor revisions); among 21 evaluated solutions from 30 open problems, 5 were completely correct, 2 more promising pending verification, and 8 contained useful partial progress.
AI.conclusion: Author-critic agentic workflows can significantly enhance LLM performance on open mathematical problems, and the agent-building library is released as open source.

title: Task-Adaptive Design of Modular Aerial Manipulators Under Airflow Exposure Constraints
comment: Accepted to the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) 2026
summary: Aerial manipulation with multirotor platforms enables physical interaction in complex environments, but rotor-induced airflow remains a critical limitation for tasks involving airflow-sensitive targets or surroundings. This paper presents an optimization-based design framework for modular aerial manipulators that jointly considers task wrench feasibility, end-effector placement, and airflow exposure constraints. We first introduce a novel categorization of target-side airflow tolerance and formulate the corresponding exposure requirements as geometric constraints. To efficiently model rotor-induced airflow, we introduce a compact cone-sphere envelope that approximates the spreading structure of a quadrotor's airflow while preserving computational tractability for optimization. Building on this formulation, we propose a reconfiguration optimization that adapts a modular aerial manipulator to diverse task wrench requirements while enforcing both target-side airflow exposure and intra-platform airflow interference constraints. Unlike prior designs that assume a fixed end-effector location, the proposed framework optimizes the end-effector placement together with the platform configuration. Scalability experiments and ablation studies validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

AI.tldr: An optimization-based design framework for modular aerial manipulators that jointly optimizes task wrench feasibility, end-effector placement, and airflow exposure constraints using a novel cone-sphere envelope for rotor-induced airflow modeling.
AI.motivation: Rotor-induced airflow from multirotor platforms limits aerial manipulation tasks involving airflow-sensitive targets or surroundings, yet prior designs assume fixed end-effector locations and neglect airflow exposure constraints.
AI.method: Introduces a categorization of target-side airflow tolerance with geometric constraint formulation, a compact cone-sphere envelope for quadrotor airflow approximation, and a reconfiguration optimization that jointly adapts end-effector placement and platform configuration under task wrench and airflow interference constraints.
AI.result: Scalability experiments and ablation studies validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables modular aerial manipulators to adapt to diverse task wrench requirements while mitigating rotor-induced airflow effects, outperforming prior fixed-end-effector designs.

title: Ceci n'est pas une pipe: AI systems as semantic abstractions
summary: An AI system's output is not the fact or world state it appears to describe, but rather an engineered representation. We propose a semantic framework to describe AI systems, to be able to examine the correctness of such representations. To do so, we distinguish what is justified by accepted domain knowledge, what reference sources say, and what the system can currently use. This allows us to give precise definitions to common failures: extrapolation, refuted or unsupported assertion, sources versus knowledge mismatch, stale or refuted source, added hypotheses, unsupported use... We hope our framework gives a useful vocabulary for specifying and checking AI systems whose outputs, citations, tool calls, and world-changing actions must be justified by reliable claims and explicit authority rather than apparent fluency.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a semantic framework for describing AI systems that distinguishes between justified knowledge, source references, and system-available information, providing precise definitions for common AI failures like extrapolation, refuted assertions, source mismatches, stale sources, and unsupported claims.
AI.motivation: AI system outputs are engineered representations rather than facts, necessitating a formal framework to examine the correctness of these representations and distinguish fluency from justified claims.
AI.method: The authors develop a semantic framework that differentiates three categories: what is justified by accepted domain knowledge, what reference sources say, and what the system can currently use. This taxonomy enables precise definitions of specific failure modes.
AI.result: Precise definitions for common AI failures: extrapolation, refuted assertion, unsupported assertion, sources versus knowledge mismatch, stale or refuted source, added hypotheses, and unsupported use.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a useful vocabulary for specifying and checking AI systems whose outputs, citations, tool calls, and actions must be justified by reliable claims and explicit authority rather than fluency.

title: CORAL-AUV: CFD Oriented Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Underwater Vehicles
summary: Fine grain control and positioning of autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) is critical for sampling, maintenance, and survey applications. Traditional control methods for AUVs are labor intensive and are not robust to changes in the vehicle configuration or environmental conditions. Reinforcement learning (RL) promises rapid controller development while handling a range of deployment parameters via domain randomization (DR). However, DR is still limited by the capacity of the underlying simulation to model real physics. In particular, drag physics are difficult to model and are a large contributor to sim-to-real gaps. Meanwhile, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) provides high fidelity drag models but is challenging to leverage within reinforcement learning frameworks due to its computational overhead. Thus, in this paper we exploit the idea of training surrogate approximations of CFD models of a given vehicle, enabling fast inference within RL pipelines. We are the first to successfully deploy a zero-shot RL policy on a 6-DOF AUV in which policy training is performed on surrogate drag models (SDMs) trained on CFD data. We find 31% lower energy usage compared to a controller using simplified physics while traversing between waypoints 11% faster with 19% less error. Our SDM based RL controller better predicts zero-shot transfer and is more robust across reward shaping design choices. When using DR to complete a task with perturbed parameters, we find that the CFD policy is the only controller that successfully transfers. The policies are evaluated in a controlled tank environment and in the field providing extensive testing of the policies' capabilities.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a reinforcement learning approach for AUV control that uses surrogate drag models trained on CFD data, achieving zero-shot deployment with lower energy usage, faster traversal, and reduced error compared to traditional methods.
AI.motivation: Fine-grained control of AUVs is critical but traditional methods are labor-intensive and not robust to changes. RL with domain randomization is promising but limited by simulation fidelity, especially drag physics. CFD provides accurate drag models but is too computationally expensive for RL pipelines.
AI.method: The authors train surrogate drag models (SDMs) from CFD data to approximate high-fidelity drag physics with fast inference, then use these SDMs within an RL training pipeline to learn a 6-DOF AUV controller, deploying it zero-shot without fine-tuning.
AI.result: The SDM-based RL controller achieves 31% lower energy usage, 11% faster waypoint traversal, and 19% less error compared to a controller using simplified physics. It also shows better zero-shot transfer robustness and is the only controller that successfully transfers under domain randomization with perturbed parameters.
AI.conclusion: Surrogate CFD-based drag models enable efficient RL training for AUV control with successful zero-shot real-world deployment, outperforming simplified physics baselines across multiple metrics.

title: Multimodal Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to align multimodal large language models (MLLMs), but higher rewards do not always imply better task performance. This risk is amplified when visual evidence is evaluated by text-only or weakly grounded rewards. We study reward hacking in MLLM RL across safety VQA, chart VQA, and stress-test settings, varying reward design, data ambiguity, model scale (2B-32B), and RL algorithm (GRPO, RLOO, DAPO). We introduce Newly Rewarded Failure Rate (NRFR), which measures failures among samples whose proxy reward improves over the SFT baseline. Outcome-only rewards cause severe hacking, reaching 48.1% Reward Hacking Rate (RHR), while NRFR exceeding RHR shows that RL creates new failures rather than merely inheriting them. Scaling reduces but does not eliminate hacking: even the 32B model retains a 54.9% worse rate under outcome-only rewards, whereas answer-aware rewards improve the oracle trend at every scale. Robustness is also algorithm- and scale-dependent: GRPO is consistently most resistant, RLOO remains vulnerable, and DAPO improves substantially from 2B to 8B. Visual-evidence rewards help only with reliable verification: keyword-based checks increase hacking, while VLM-as-judge semantic verification reduces it. Overall, multimodal reward hacking is a systematic result of optimizing imperfect rewards, and robust alignment requires rewards and verifiers that remain reliable under optimization pressure.

AI.tldr: Multimodal reward hacking in MLLM RL is systematic: outcome-only rewards cause up to 48.1% RHR, NRFR reveals new failures created by RL rather than inherited, scaling reduces but does not eliminate hacking, GRPO is most robust, and visual rewards only help with reliable semantic verification.
AI.motivation: RL is increasingly used to align MLLMs, but higher rewards do not always imply better task performance, especially when visual evidence is evaluated by text-only or weakly grounded rewards. The risk of reward hacking in multimodal settings is understudied.
AI.method: The authors study reward hacking across safety VQA, chart VQA, and stress-test settings, varying reward design, data ambiguity, model scale (2B-32B), and RL algorithms (GRPO, RLOO, DAPO). They introduce Newly Rewarded Failure Rate (NRFR) to measure failures among samples whose proxy reward improves over the SFT baseline.
AI.result: Outcome-only rewards cause severe hacking (48.1% RHR). NRFR exceeding RHR shows RL creates new failures rather than inheriting them. Scaling reduces but does not eliminate hacking (32B model retains 54.9% worse rate under outcome-only rewards). GRPO is most resistant, RLOO vulnerable, DAPO improves from 2B to 8B. Keyword-based visual rewards increase hacking; VLM-as-judge semantic verification reduces it.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal reward hacking is a systematic result of optimizing imperfect rewards; robust alignment requires rewards and verifiers that remain reliable under optimization pressure.

title: CoDiMAD: Diffusion-Based Privileged Distillation for Communication-Free Multi-Robot Coordination
summary: Decentralized multi-robot coordination under partial observability remains challenging, especially in communication-free settings where agents must act solely from local sensor observations. Privileged policy distillation provides a promising approach by transferring knowledge from a globally informed oracle to sensor-constrained students. However, in multi-agent systems, the same local observation may correspond to multiple global configurations requiring qualitatively different cooperative actions, making the conditional action distribution inherently multi-modal. Standard deterministic distillation collapses these modes to their mean, often yielding invalid or hesitant actions. To address this issue, we propose CoDiMAD, a three-stage framework that trains a privileged oracle with MAPPO, constructs an offline dataset of local-observation-oracle-action pairs, and distills the oracle into decentralized students parameterized as conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic models. By approximating the conditional oracle-action distribution through the diffusion reverse process, CoDiMAD samples decisive actions from coherent coordination modes rather than averaging across them. Theoretical analysis characterizes the mode-averaging failure of deterministic distillation and the distributional recovery property of diffusion-based distillation. Experiments on three cooperative tasks show that CoDiMAD consistently outperforms direct local MARL and deterministic distillation baselines. The source code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: CoDiMAD uses diffusion-based privileged policy distillation to learn decentralized multi-robot coordination from a globally informed oracle, overcoming the mode-averaging failure of deterministic distillation in multi-modal action distributions under partial observability.
AI.motivation: Decentralized multi-robot coordination under partial observability and communication-free settings is challenging. Privileged policy distillation can transfer knowledge from an oracle to sensor-constrained students, but in multi-agent systems, the same local observation can correspond to multiple global configurations requiring different cooperative actions (multi-modal conditional distribution). Standard deterministic distillation collapses these modes to their mean, producing invalid or hesitant actions.
AI.method: Three-stage framework: (1) Train a privileged oracle with MAPPO (multi-agent PPO). (2) Construct an offline dataset of local-observation–oracle-action pairs. (3) Distill the oracle into decentralized students modeled as conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs), which approximate the conditional oracle-action distribution via the diffusion reverse process, enabling sampling of decisive actions from coherent coordination modes.
AI.result: Experiments on three cooperative tasks show CoDiMAD consistently outperforms direct local MARL and deterministic distillation baselines. Theoretical analysis characterizes mode-averaging failure of deterministic distillation and the distributional recovery property of diffusion-based distillation.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion-based privileged policy distillation (CoDiMAD) effectively addresses multi-modality in decentralized multi-robot coordination under partial observability, providing a principled way to avoid mode collapse and produce coherent cooperative behaviors without communication.

title: Shared Selective Persistent Memory for Agentic LLM Systems
summary: Agentic LLM systems that generate code through multi-turn tool use face a fundamental context problem: each session starts from zero, discarding the configuration choices, domain constraints, data schemas, and tool-use patterns that made previous sessions productive. Naively persisting entire conversation histories is token-inefficient and counterproductive: irrelevant context degrades generation quality. We introduce shared selective persistent memory, an architecture that identifies and retains four categories of reusable context (task specifications, data schemas, tool configurations, and output constraints) while discarding session-specific reasoning traces. Crucially, this memory is shared: workspaces encapsulating selective memory can be transferred across users with role-based access control, enabling collaborative reuse without redundant specification. We implement it in a deployed collaborative workspace platform where LLM agents produce, edit, and maintain git-versioned artifacts (dashboards, reports, and data-driven documents) from heterogeneous sources (CSV, SQL, REST APIs, and MCP servers). A complementary zero-token data refresh mechanism decouples generated programs from runtime data, enabling artifact reuse without re-invocation. Across three enterprise scenarios, shared selective persistent memory achieves 96% task completion (vs. 79% without memory and 71% with full history). Zero-token refresh eliminates LLM re-invocation for recurring updates (14x task-time reduction), while summary-driven generation cuts per-invocation token cost by 97x versus raw data injection. A replication on four public datasets confirms generalizability, with zero-token refresh succeeding in 12/12 trials. Notably, naive full-history persistence actively degrades completion by biasing the agent with stale traces, while selective memory outperforms both extremes.

AI.tldr: Introduces shared selective persistent memory (SSPM) for agentic LLM systems that retains reusable context (task specs, data schemas, tool configs, output constraints) while discarding session-specific reasoning, achieving 96% task completion, 97x token cost reduction, and 14x task-time reduction across enterprise scenarios.
AI.motivation: Agentic LLM systems generating code through multi-turn tool use start each session from scratch, discarding reusable context (configurations, constraints, schemas, patterns) from prior sessions. Naive full-history persistence is token-inefficient and degrades generation quality due to irrelevant context.
AI.method: Proposes shared selective persistent memory architecture that identifies and retains four categories of reusable context (task specifications, data schemas, tool configurations, output constraints) while discarding session-specific reasoning traces. Memory is shared across users via role-based access control. Includes a zero-token data refresh mechanism decoupling generated programs from runtime data.
AI.result: 96% task completion (vs. 79% without memory, 71% with full history). Zero-token refresh achieves 14x task-time reduction. Summary-driven generation cuts token cost 97x vs. raw data injection. Replication on 4 public datasets: zero-token refresh succeeds 12/12 trials. Full-history persistence actively degrades completion.
AI.conclusion: Selective persistent memory significantly outperforms both no-memory and full-history approaches for agentic LLM systems. Zero-token refresh enables efficient recurring updates without LLM re-invocation. The architecture is generalizable and deployed in a collaborative workspace platform.

title: PAC-ACT: Post-training Actor-Critic for Action Chunking Transformers
summary: Precision industrial contact manipulation requires reliable robot policies under pose perturbations and contact-force constraints. Vision-language-action models offer broad generalization but often introduce high inference latency and GPU-memory cost, while vision-action chunking policies are more suitable for real-time industrial control. However, these policies are usually trained by behavior cloning and suffer from distribution shift in contact-rich tasks. This paper proposes PAC-ACT, a reinforcement-learning post-training framework for pretrained Action Chunking Transformer policies. PAC-ACT reformulates policy optimization at the chunk level, constructs an ACT-transferred actor-critic architecture, and introduces a hybrid behavior-prior constraint to preserve the pretrained action distribution during online fine-tuning. Experiments on industrial precision-contact benchmarks show that PAC-ACT improves task success, contact stability, and force safety while retaining low latency and low GPU-memory usage. On the Contour task, PAC-ACT significantly reduces peak contact force and decreases the proportion of force readings above 60 N by 46 times. Sparse-reward ablations further show that the proposed behavior-prior constraint enables effective exploration under randomized initial poses.

AI.tldr: PAC-ACT is a reinforcement-learning post-training framework that refines pretrained Action Chunking Transformer policies for precision industrial contact manipulation, improving task success, contact stability, and force safety while maintaining low latency and low GPU-memory usage.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-language-action models offer generalization but have high latency and GPU-memory costs, while vision-action chunking policies (more suitable for real-time control) suffer from distribution shift under contact-rich tasks due to behavior cloning training.
AI.method: PAC-ACT reformulates policy optimization at the chunk level, constructs an ACT-transferred actor-critic architecture, and introduces a hybrid behavior-prior constraint to preserve the pretrained action distribution during online fine-tuning.
AI.result: On the Contour task, PAC-ACT reduces peak contact force and decreases the proportion of force readings above 60 N by 46 times. Sparse-reward ablations show the behavior-prior constraint enables effective exploration under randomized initial poses.
AI.conclusion: PAC-ACT improves task success, contact stability, and force safety in industrial precision-contact benchmarks while retaining low latency and low GPU-memory usage, making it suitable for real-time industrial contact manipulation.

title: SAGEAgent: A Self-Evolving Agent for Cost-Aware Modality Acquisition in Multimodal Survival Prediction
summary: Does every cancer patient truly need a complete diagnostic workup for accurate survival prediction? In multimodal clinical oncology, diagnostic modalities follow a clinically mandated order of escalating burden -- from demographics collected at intake to genomic profiling requiring specialized tissue analysis. Current multimodal survival methods either assume all modalities are available or passively handle missing data, but none actively reason about whether acquiring the next modality is justified for a given patient along this ordered workflow. We formulate this as a sequential decision problem and propose SAGEAgent (Sequential Acquisition Guided by Experience), a self-evolving LLM-based clinical agent that decides which diagnostic modalities to acquire for each patient, balancing predictive accuracy against clinical invasiveness. SAGEAgent reasons about each patient's evolving diagnostic state through clinical tools that translate numerical predictions into text, an episodic memory that retrieves similar past cases, and a semantic memory that accumulates reusable decision patterns from experience. Experiments on a glioma cohort combining TCGA-LGG, TCGA-GBM, and BraTS with four diagnostic modalities demonstrate that SAGEAgent achieves competitive survival prediction accuracy while reducing average acquisition burden by 55%.

AI.tldr: SAGEAgent is an LLM-based clinical agent that sequentially decides which diagnostic modalities to acquire for each cancer patient, reducing acquisition burden by 55% while maintaining competitive survival prediction accuracy.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal survival methods assume all modalities are available or passively handle missing data, but none actively reason about whether acquiring the next, more invasive diagnostic modality is justified for a given patient along the clinically mandated workflow.
AI.method: Formulated as a sequential decision problem using an LLM-based agent with clinical tools (translating numerical predictions to text), episodic memory (retrieving similar past cases), and semantic memory (accumulating reusable decision patterns).
AI.result: On a glioma cohort (TCGA-LGG, TCGA-GBM, BraTS) with four diagnostic modalities, SAGEAgent achieved competitive survival prediction accuracy while reducing average acquisition burden by 55%.
AI.conclusion: Not all patients need a complete diagnostic workup; sequential, intelligent modality acquisition can substantially reduce clinical burden without sacrificing prediction accuracy.

title: B-spline Policy: Accelerating Manipulation Policies via B-spline Action Representations
summary: In this work, we present B-spline Policy (BSP), an action representation designed for accelerating robot manipulation policies. Rather than predicting discrete-time action chunks, BSP parameterizes actions as continuous B-spline curves defined by a set of knots and control points. This representation yields smooth, time-continuous trajectories that can be temporally scaled and executed by low-level controllers at higher frequencies and speeds. We show that B-spline-parameterized actions can be seamlessly integrated into standard policy learning pipelines by directly predicting B-spline parameters. Experiments on simulated and real-world tasks demonstrate that BSP significantly reduces task completion time, achieving substantial improvements over baseline methods while maintaining strong success rates. More results: https://b-spline-policy.github.io

AI.tldr: B-spline Policy (BSP) replaces discrete action chunks with continuous B-spline curves for robot manipulation, enabling smoother, faster, and temporally scalable actions that reduce task completion time while maintaining high success rates.
AI.motivation: Accelerating robot manipulation policies by overcoming the limitations of discrete-time action chunk predictions, which are temporally rigid and cannot be smoothly scaled or executed at higher frequencies.
AI.method: BSP parameterizes actions as continuous B-spline curves defined by knots and control points. The B-spline parameters are directly predicted within standard policy learning pipelines, and the resulting smooth trajectories can be executed by low-level controllers at higher frequencies and speeds with temporal scaling.
AI.result: Significant reduction in task completion time with substantial improvements over baseline methods on both simulated and real-world tasks, while maintaining strong success rates.
AI.conclusion: B-spline-parameterized action representation is an effective approach for accelerating robot manipulation, offering smoothness, temporal scalability, and seamless integration into existing policy learning frameworks.

title: Beyond Fixed Representations: The Vocabulary and Verifier Gaps in Open-Ended AI
summary:
Modern AI systems are increasingly being evaluated for their ability to reason, code, prove theorems, use tools, and long-horizon research tasks. These are powerful capabilities, but they share a structural limitation: the representational frame within which the model operates, including its conceptual vocabulary, the space of admissible solutions it can search, and the criteria by which success is evaluated, is typically fixed and supplied in advance. This paper argues that building stronger intelligent systems capable of open-ended innovation requires additional classes of operations: the creation, stabilization, and reuse of new representational primitives, which alter the space being searched rather than simply searching within it.
  We characterize the distance between current AI systems and genuinely open-ended intelligence through two gaps. The first is the vocabulary gap, the difficulty of inventing and stabilizing new representational primitives rather than merely recombining existing ones. The second is the verifier gap, the difficulty of judging the value of a new primitive when its full payoff may be visible only after future reuse. We interpret both gaps through a unified framework of intelligence as cognitive discrepancy reduction. By viewing intelligent behaviors as a sequence of cognitive transformations, we distinguish intra-space transformations which operate within a fixed representational frame, from generative transformations which may modify the frame itself. On this basis, we propose a ladder of innovation autonomy and outline several directions for advancing open-ended AI, including objectives that reward useful representational change, persistent memory architectures for invented primitives, and adaptive verification mechanisms capable of evolving alongside the representations they evaluate.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies two gaps—the vocabulary gap (inventing new representational primitives) and the verifier gap (evaluating novel primitives whose value emerges only through future reuse)—that separate current AI from open-ended intelligence, and proposes a framework of cognitive discrepancy reduction with a ladder of innovation autonomy to guide progress.
AI.motivation: Current AI systems operate within fixed representational frames (fixed conceptual vocabularies, solution spaces, and success criteria), which limits their capacity for open-ended innovation. The paper aims to characterize and bridge the gap between these systems and genuinely open-ended intelligence.
AI.method: The paper introduces two gaps—vocabulary gap (difficulty of inventing/stabilizing new representational primitives) and verifier gap (difficulty of evaluating primitives whose value depends on future reuse). It unifies these via a cognitive discrepancy reduction framework, distinguishing intra-space (fixed frame) from generative (frame-modifying) transformations, and proposes a ladder of innovation autonomy.
AI.result: A conceptual framework distinguishing intra-space from generative transformations, a ladder of innovation autonomy, and three proposed directions: objectives rewarding useful representational change, persistent memory architectures for invented primitives, and adaptive verification mechanisms that co-evolve with representations.
AI.conclusion: Advancing open-ended AI requires enabling systems to create, stabilize, and reuse new representational primitives that alter the search space itself, rather than only searching within a fixed space. The vocabulary and verifier gaps must be addressed through new objectives, architectures, and verification mechanisms.

title: Knowledge Graphs and Explainable AI as Complementary Resources for Urban Mining
comment: Accepted for presentation at the AISE Workshop @ IJCAI-ECAI 2026
summary: Pre-demolition assessment, the regulated audit process at the heart of urban mining, is an information process in which AI support must serve qualified auditors who remain accountable for the decisions taken. The relevant unit of value is not prediction accuracy alone, but the defensibility of the supported decisions: their legibility, plausibility, sourcing, and contestability. Explainable AI techniques and domain knowledge graphs each address parts of this requirement, and existing taxonomies have catalogued their integration. The literature is descriptively rich but structurally under-specified: what remains less developed is a structural account of why specific integrations produce artefacts neither resource can provide alone. This paper offers a complementarity-theoretic interpretation grounded in the IS resource-based tradition. We propose four consolidated KG-XAI integration modes (Lifting, Constraining, Typing, and Revising), each defined as a typed operation over XAI artefacts and knowledge-graph substrate structures. Each mode unlocks a distinct property of defensibility and contributes to the kind of regulatory artefact pre-demolition assessment demands. A fire-door example from the urban-mining process illustrates the modes using the W3C Linked Building Data stack and valuation extensions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a complementarity-theoretic framework integrating Knowledge Graphs (KG) and Explainable AI (XAI) for defensible decision support in pre-demolition assessment (urban mining). It identifies four integration modes—Lifting, Constraining, Typing, Revising—that each unlock distinct properties of defensibility (legibility, plausibility, sourcing, contestability). The framework is illustrated with a fire-door example using W3C Linked Building Data.
AI.motivation: Current AI support for pre-demolition assessment (urban mining) focuses narrowly on prediction accuracy, but the regulatory audit context requires defensible decisions (legible, plausible, sourced, contestable). While KG-XAI integrations have been taxonomically catalogued, no structural account explains why specific integrations produce artefacts neither resource alone can provide.
AI.method: The authors develop a complementarity-theoretic interpretation grounded in the IS resource-based tradition, proposing four consolidated KG-XAI integration modes: Lifting, Constraining, Typing, and Revising. Each mode is defined as a typed operation over XAI artefacts and knowledge-graph substrate structures. The approach is illustrated with a fire-door example from urban mining using the W3C Linked Building Data stack and valuation extensions.
AI.result: Four KG-XAI integration modes are proposed: Lifting, Constraining, Typing, and Revising. Each mode unlocks a distinct property of defensibility (legibility, plausibility, sourcing, contestability) and contributes to the kind of regulatory artefact that pre-demolition assessment requires. The modes are demonstrated via a concrete fire-door example using standardised building data semantics.
AI.conclusion: The complementarity-theoretic framework provides a structurally under-specified gap in the KG-XAI integration literature. The four modes offer a principled basis for designing AI support that serves human auditors in high-accountability regulatory settings, moving beyond prediction accuracy toward defensibility as the relevant unit of value.

title: TrustX Agent Risk Classification Framework (ARC): Risk-Tiering Internally Created Agentic AI Systems
comment: This is a working paper on our risk classification tool, with iterations currently underway
summary: The proliferation of agentic AI systems across enterprise and public-sector contexts has outpaced the capacity of general-purpose AI risk frameworks to classify and govern them. In this paper, we introduce the TrustX Agent Risk Classification Framework, a structured, repeatable instrument that can be applied to seven types of agentic AI systems and is grounded in foundational pre-existing AI governance frameworks. At the core of the framework is a twelve-dimension scoring rubric that robustly quantifies the risk. This rubric is combined with other components, such as the GPA + IAT classification model and the five-level autonomy framework derived from existing literature. These inputs produce a three-tier governance output with mapped control recommendations. A specialised Coding Assistant extension is also included to account for nuances specific to this type of agentic AI system. We then use an illustrative example to show our framework in practice. ARC is intended for AI governance practitioners, risk officers, developers, and regulators, and it will regularly undergo iteration as we continue to expand it and make it more robust. The community can access the interactive framework here: https://arc.responsible.ai/

AI.tldr: Introduces the TrustX Agent Risk Classification Framework (ARC), a structured instrument for classifying and governing risk across seven types of agentic AI systems, featuring a twelve-dimension scoring rubric, GPA+IAT classification model, five-level autonomy framework, and three-tier governance output with control recommendations, plus a Coding Assistant extension.
AI.motivation: The rapid deployment of agentic AI systems across enterprise and public sectors has outpaced the ability of existing general-purpose AI risk frameworks to adequately classify and govern them.
AI.method: A structured, repeatable risk classification framework grounded in pre-existing AI governance frameworks, comprising: (1) a twelve-dimension scoring rubric for quantifying risk, (2) a GPA+IAT classification model, (3) a five-level autonomy framework from existing literature, and (4) a three-tier governance output with mapped control recommendations. A specialized Coding Assistant extension addresses domain-specific nuances.
AI.result: Produces a three-tier governance output with mapped control recommendations, demonstrated via an illustrative example. An interactive framework is publicly accessible.
AI.conclusion: ARC is intended for AI governance practitioners, risk officers, developers, and regulators, with plans for regular iteration to enhance robustness and expand coverage.

title: Agora: Enhancing LLM Agent Reasoning Via Auction-Based Task Allocation
summary: Enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language model (LLM) agents requires effective orchestration of diverse expert models and tools. However, existing frameworks typically call APIs based on coarse-grained matching between tasks and the functions of expert models or tools, while overlooking critical factors such as performance variability and cost efficiency among functionally similar alternatives. To address this, we propose Agora, a framework that introduces an incentive-compatible auction mechanism for dynamically allocating tasks to expert models and tools. By treating reasoning steps as tradeable items, Agora enables agents to bid based on their rectified competence-ensuring that critical logic is routed to the most capable solver rather than the most overconfident one. Evaluations across five benchmarks show that Agora improves over matched single-model, routing, and cascade baselines under comparable candidate pools, while exposing a controllable cost-quality trade-off through a single auction parameter.

AI.tldr: Agora is an auction-based framework that dynamically allocates tasks to expert models and tools by treating reasoning steps as tradeable items, using rectified competence bids to route critical logic to the most capable solver, improving reasoning performance across five benchmarks with controllable cost-quality trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent frameworks rely on coarse-grained task-function matching for API calls, ignoring performance variability and cost efficiency among functionally similar expert models and tools, leading to suboptimal orchestration.
AI.method: Introduces an incentive-compatible auction mechanism where reasoning steps are treated as tradeable items; agents bid based on rectified competence, ensuring critical logic is routed to the most capable solver rather than the most overconfident one.
AI.result: Evaluated across five benchmarks, Agora outperforms matched single-model, routing, and cascade baselines under comparable candidate pools, with a controllable cost-quality trade-off via a single auction parameter.
AI.conclusion: Agora effectively enhances LLM agent reasoning by dynamically and cost-efficiently allocating tasks to expert models/tools through an auction mechanism that accounts for competence and cost.

title: ConceptSMILE: Auditing the Trustworthiness of Concept-Based Explainable AI
summary: Concept-based explainable artificial intelligence (AI) can make model reasoning more human-understandable, but concept-level outputs are not automatically trustworthy. We introduce ConceptSMILE, a model-agnostic perturbation-based auditing framework for evaluating the reliability of concept-based explanations. Rather than replacing SMILE, ConceptSMILE extends its perturbation-based logic from feature- or region-level attribution to the auditing of human-understandable concept explanations. The framework perturbs input regions, measures concept-response shifts, applies locality weighting, and fits an XGBoost surrogate to approximate local concept behaviour. Reliability is assessed through attribution accuracy, surrogate fidelity, faithfulness, stability, and consistency. We evaluate ConceptSMILE on retinal fundus images by comparing MedSAM-derived visual concepts with VLM-based semantic concepts. Results show that reliability varies across concepts and pathways: MedSAM achieves stronger spatial attribution and the highest surrogate fidelity ($R^2 = 0.8503$, $R_w^2 = 0.8465$), while the VLM pathway shows stronger vessel faithfulness and stronger stability under selected artefact conditions. ConceptSMILE provides an independent audit layer for evaluating the trustworthiness of concept-based XAI.

AI.tldr: ConceptSMILE is a perturbation-based auditing framework that evaluates the reliability of concept-based explanations in XAI, tested on retinal fundus images comparing MedSAM and VLM concepts across five reliability metrics.
AI.motivation: Concept-based XAI can improve interpretability, but concept-level outputs are not inherently trustworthy. There lacks a systematic auditing method to evaluate the reliability of such explanations.
AI.method: ConceptSMILE perturbs input regions, measures concept-response shifts, applies locality weighting, and fits an XGBoost surrogate to approximate local concept behavior. Reliability is assessed via attribution accuracy, surrogate fidelity, faithfulness, stability, and consistency.
AI.result: MedSAM achieves stronger spatial attribution and highest surrogate fidelity (R²=0.8503, R²_w=0.8465); VLM pathway shows stronger vessel faithfulness and stronger stability under selected artefact conditions. Reliability varies across concepts and pathways.
AI.conclusion: ConceptSMILE provides an independent audit layer for evaluating the trustworthiness of concept-based XAI, revealing that reliability is not uniform and depends on the concept extraction method and pathway.
